title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 37: Kellar's Keep and Purge the Foe
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I talked about some hobby work and my final list for Challenger's Cup this weekend. As this publishes, I'll be on my way to Salt Lake City for this weekend's event. But I also had a packed weekend - I was able to get in a practice game with my new Thousand Sons list and another round of HeroQuest.

Kickstarting Kellar's Keep

Last week we kicked off Kellar's Keep with the kids, running the bridge mission The Forsaken Tunnels of Xor-Xel. We added a new player and ended up having a great time. This week she was back and we ran the campaign proper, doing the Great Gate mission. I've wanted to start ramping up the roleplaying aspects for a while as a way to introduce some non-combat activity to the game and this was a great opportunity. This time around I created an Imperial campsite for them waiting on the other side of the tunnels.

The idea here is that the king's forces are deep in the keep, beset by enemy forces. What's left is a small scouting force holding the camp outside the Great Gate. Sergeant Brannik is the leftover leader of those forces, and he's holding down the camp. The other major NPC here is Pell the cook, stirring a pot of onions and regret.

Sergeant Brannik

The kids dropped in and I instructed them that this was a bit of a different scenario. They'd tell me what their characters do and say what they say. If they talk to Pell, he can give them information about the king and his army, and share some of his soup. If they talk more than once, he'd eventually give them potions of healing as a reward. I took the opportunity to do some custom props for this:

I grabbed the bottles from my dad, who I think had them from a wine of the day thing someone bought him for Christmas. I washed them out and filled them with a mix of Gatorade and Sprite to give them a bubbly texture. It turned out to be a big hit with the kids, who really liked it and thought the props were great. They also looked awesome.

If they talk to Brannik multiple times, the gruff old Dwarf scout will hand them the tattered remains of a map drawn by his scouts. The map has a warning about a trap in the dungeon and the location of some secret doors. It's another cool prop, made by soaking a piece of paper in coffee, then baking it at 350 degrees for a few minutes until it dried. Then I scrabbled some notes on it and added some bloody fingerprints by dipping my fingers in some Blood for the Blood God.

On the whole, it was a great session and the kids had a great time. I once again was reminded that children are psychopaths; two of them wanted to do fun roleplay stuff - Bryce announced that he was a brave barbarian of the north, here to avenge his people and bring honor to their memory. The girl playing the monk immediately informed me that "her character was bored" and "immediately wanted to windmill kick sergeant Brannik in the face."

No notes, 10/10 experience.

Practice Game: vs. Andrew's Astra Militarum

With the second half of my Labor Day, I had my buddy Andrew over for a game. He's also going to Challenger's Cup, playing on team Sanctum. He was free on Labor day so he came over for a quick test game before we went over to my folks' house for some burgers and dogs.

This was Purge the Foe (me) vs. Recon, which I think leans toward Purge but the list matchup is tough - Andrew's definitely got the kind of list filled with tough, medium targets that take a lot of firepower to bring down but not an entire terminator unit. This makes spittling fire very tricky and means Andrew has more staying power than I'd like.

Andrew gets first turn and plays it safe, keeping back. I return the favor and step forward and score some early kill secondary points but generally also try to avoid getting shot first by a bunch of Leman Russ tanks. Andrew pushes up on his second turn and I ingress one unit of Terminators, and Andrew manages to take out one of my Rubric units - and I forget to change the dead character into a spawn.

On the following turn I'll kill three tanks and press forward. I had a really bad round with my rituals, but ultimately I was able to put Andrew on the back foot. That said, the back foot isn't dead, and Andrew put in some work against my surviving Scarabs, winnowing them down a bit with a mix of fire from Kasrkin and Leman Russ tanks. The upside is that I get models back with the Ritual of Regeneration. My goal from here is to keep picking up tanks and use the Tzaangors to threaten Andrew's backfield. I control the middle pretty well and he'll be feeding me tanks but as the Terminators lose models they'll struggle to kill a Leman Russ. I need to drop two more on my next turn.

I was in a good place to win the game after round 3 - I had good position and better presence with my units, plus I'd Consecrated three objectives. That said, preventing a triple triangulation is also more or less impossible, but I was ahead on secondaries. If we were playing singles, this would have been great. But we were playing teams practice, and my goal is to win with 15+ while Andrew's army is focused on keeping it close. I probably win this one 11-9 or 12-8 if we keep playing it, but that's a win for Andrew, especially if he can keep it close enough for a 10-10.

Result: Draw, kind of

And that was the game. We called it early to go over to my parents' house for some cookout - dad made burgs and dogs on the grill. It wasn't the first time Andrew's been to my folks' place for dinner; we normally do Sunday night family dinners but guests are invited so anyone hanging out on Sunday is welcome. But this particular weekend we held it for Monday.

In all, a great Labor Day game.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. Wish me luck at Challenger's Cup this weekend - we'll need it, but we also won't make any good use of it. We're not going to win or sniff a podium, but we're guaranteed to have a good time regardless. As usual, the worst part of a Warhammer weekend figures to be the actual games of Warhammer. Which less an indictment of Warhammer and more an indication of how much fun hanging out with my friends in a rental house is.

See you next Thursday.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: [Warmachine] Going NOVA: Sea Raiders Invade Virginia
content:
I spent most of this long Labor Day weekend trekking down to the Warmachine events at NOVA, the Northern Virginia tabletop convention.  This superlative convention hosted in Washington DC hosts all sorts of tabletop games and Warmachine was well-attended this year.  Boasting two Steamrollers, an Iron Gauntlet Qualifier, a team tournament and a narrative event over the course of four days, there was truly something for everyone who wanted to bring focus and fury to the table.  Special acknowledgements to Tried & True for running such a successful series of events and of course all of their contributors in terrain donations, streaming, prize support and running/judging the main and side events to keep things running smooth.

Credit: Blake

I played in three different events over the course of the weekend: The Thursday Night Last Chance Steamroller, the Iron Gauntlet Qualifier (games Friday and Sunday) and the Nova Team Tournament on team Donut Holes.  Besides having some awesome games and immersing myself in this great community, my intent was to hone my WTC list contenders to a knife's edge.  Thus, for simplicity purposes, I brought all of the same lists to each event:

Thursday Night: The Last Chance Everyone's Qualified Steamroller

Longshanks here.

Despite the name, the only last chance in this steamroller was a chance to practice before the next day's Iron Gauntlet.  I intended to use this event for warm-ups/practice and dropped after two rounds, as I figured extra sleep would be more valuable for the next day of the Iron Gauntlet

Round 1: Butcher vs. Stormcraw (Kithguard) on Wolves At Our Heels

This game was fairly well defined around a large obstruction in the middle that bisected the 50mm objectives.  My opponent went second and chose the more defensive side that allowed his Guard Tower to go behind the obstruction.  Stormcraw and his heavier elements (Steelbacks, Ramhead and his Mistborn) favored the left side of the table with some lighter elements covering the right and the Scrappers and Throat Cutters in ambush, deploying opposite my left side Rhoks and right side warjacks, with Constance and Gallant and my Assault Reavers up the middle.

My first turn was spent running up aggressively as Butcher does.  Stormcraw feated on turn 1 to attempt to aggressively leverage his ambush threats on the first scoring turn, but unfortunately my opponent underestimated how aggressive I was going to be.  Butcher feated top of 2 targeting my Rhoks with Horn of Woe in order for them to charge, take out Ramhead, and then reposition to surround his left-side Trapdoor and prevent it from being used to Ambush.  My right side models took out his Spirit Shamans on his 40mm as well as his Sidewinder, with the Assault Reavers moving up to take down the Guard Tower and surround his remaining trapdoors along with my repositioning Barragers.  Constance and Gallant moved up to ensure they could benefit from as much Requiem as possible for Stormcraw's counterattack.

Credit: Blake

Stormcraw's feat was unimpressive by design, forcing him to change plans by deploying the Scrappers to threaten my 40mm objective while the Throat Cutters deployed to his own.  The Steelbacks killed several of the Rhok Harriers used to kill Ramhead, enough so that the Scrappers could move to take my 40mm.  Stormcraw and the Mistborn moved up to take down my Assault Reavers, although he had no mechanism for moving Constance out of contesting range.  The Jungle Troll moved up to intercept my warjacks on the other side of the obstruction.

Turn 3 saw Constance at maximum Requiem go in on Stormcraw, the Mistborn, and a single Kithguard Medic.  The Mistborn was the only transfer target, so my intention was to deal as much damage as possible to Stormcraw and maybe force a few transfers to the Mistborn, who would also be suffering damage, followed by Careful Recon to get Constance out of the way to make room for Gallant to try to finish off Stormcraw.  It didn't come to that, however, as Constance's attacks (1 initial attack and 3 Flashing Blades, all with Divine Inspiration and Boosted Damage) quickly cut through his transfers, with Constance's final strike showing me triple 6s for a photo finish.

The photo finish!  Credit: Blake

Round 2: Butcher vs. Craghorn (Kithguard) on Two Fronts

Was not expecting two Kithguard games in one day, especially against my fellow Donut Holes teammate!  I didn't know Craghorn especially well except as the ambush specialist, which certainly made me worry a bit on Two Fronts.  Fortunately, I got to go second and choose a relatively secure 40mm point as well as making the flag terrain a large obstruction near it, making it difficult for either of us to secure and ensuring that the game would be more closely decided by the 50mm objectives, where I felt I had an advantage.

After initial trapdoor entries, he had Throat Cutters, a unit of Kithguard Infantry, 2 Mortar Teams and a Sidewinder lying in wait.  His turn 2 was unexpectedly aggressive with his other Kithguard Infantry unit going to a charge on my Assault Reavers to apply Countermeasures to my army, though his poor dice and my use of Last Word limited the actual damage.  My turn 2 consisted of Butcher wiping out the infantry in the middle and feating on the Rhoks once again to attempt to eliminate his Steelbacks with just an advance since he kept them out of line of sight for charge attacks, though they only killed two.  Constance and Gallant moved to aggressively contest his 50mm with my Flail Tyrant playing backup.

His Turn 3 feat turn brought on his Kithguard Infantry off the side to kill one of my Rhok units as well as my Barragers on the right side while the Throat Cutters and Sidewinder emerged on the left to weaken Gallant enough that Ramhead was able to kill it, although he was unable to finish off Constance.  My counterattack got the Rhoks into the Kithguard infantry to kill most of them with lucky throws, while Butcher himself dove into the Throat Cutters and killed them all to control the far side 50mm while my Tyrant killed Ramhead with Redline and Hand of Destruction.  At that point, only token contesting with his remaining ambushing weapon crew was possible and I took it on scenario.

Shout-out to the crazy late-night 3-0s in that one.  For my part, I was getting a little shut-eye in preparation for...

Friday and Sunday: NOVA Iron Gauntlet Qualifier

Longshanks here.

Round 1: Butcher vs. Vallyx (Shadowflame Shard) on High Stakes

Playing against another Donut Holes teammate, this game quickly turned aggressive as we constantly fought over the middle objective.  He quickly committed his Trikhymaerex to kill Gallant and secure the 50mm, which I counter-took with a feated Tyrant, meaning that the game devolved into a slog where control of the 50mm was trading back and forth.

My opponent's scenario terrain was a wall template that was fairly close to the middle of the table and so my opponent secured it aggressively with Incarnate Knights and ultimately Vallyx personally.  It was also the first piece to "explode" and represented the first significant scenario lead of the game.  Butcher took on the right side of the board, killing a Vypex and his Talons that committed to kill a Tyrant and Constance while keeping a safe distance from Vallyx.  My Barragers on my further-back scenario terrain point scored it more consistently than his easily contestable scenario piece as his ambushing Wind Strikers were his only real contesting models and they were dispatched in quick order.

The game went a full seven turns and all three of the scenario terrain pieces "exploded" during the game, the final one being my own piece at the bottom of turn 7, which I had anticipated and had used Duck and Cover to Dig In my Barragers the turn earlier.  A wild back-and-forth game that gave me no time to rest before I jumped straight into round 2.

Round 2: Kishtaar vs. Bohdan (Old Umbrey) on Trench Warfare

Bohdan got to go second on Trench Warfare, which is a significant advantage, but I had played into Old Umbrey enough to know that Kishtaar has ridiculous advantage into this matchup, as Bohdan's shooting defenses are nearly nonexistent and it's difficult for him to apply Incite profitably without risking sudden death.  My Tyrants moved up to protect my cache and Arcane Vortex meant he couldn't manipulate a charge onto them with Winged Nuisance.  He committed his Primeval to the left side 50mm and committed his Feral to take the right side, while the Starved took the middle in hopes that the obstruction cover would save it.

Credit: Blake

My feat barrage killed the Starved, the Liegeman Ursans on the right and exhausted all of his Shield Guard bears, forcing a fairly complete collapse of the right side of the board apart from the Hounds and Feral, who did work under Incite buffs to kill a Tyrant and the Execrators.  Being left with fewer attacks meant that my remaining Assault Reavers on that side were able to jump on the Trench Warfare Scenario Terrain at a critical moment and pull ahead in points.  Bohdan focused his influence more centrally and on the right side, which meant the left side was a slower grind with his Liegeman Cavalry and Primeval unable to finish off my Sure Foot Assault Reavers and dispatching the Primeval over 2 turns of shooting.  Ultimately, once I finished off the Primeval and Feral and Bohdan's feat was exhausted, there was nothing left to keep him out of the crosshairs of my remaining shooting.

Round 3: Butcher vs. Tyrus (House Kallyss) on Fault Lines

This match was streamed live, although perhaps it's better if it wasn't.  The Tyrus list was the 30 soulless model variety, backed up by three Ghasts to enable Flank, Lanyssa and her pet cats, and essential support to strike fast and hard with the swarm of dudes.  I went second and watched the wave of Soulless run up to me, though keeping a healthy distance from Butcher.  As Butcher could kill them all himself, but cannot outthreat them between the Dusk speed buffs and his army's innate resistance to Hunter's Mark, I did a risky play, giving Butcher Stand Your Ground and riding up to the forefront of the army on full focus camp backed up by the Revenant Champion to threaten his 40mm objectives, daring him to commit or retreat his masses of elves and counting on my surrounding models, good stats, and spell immunity to limit his damage.  Still, as the old saying goes: "The risk was calculated, but man am I bad at math."

It was at this point that Orsus regretted everything.  Credit: The Ice King

The factor that I did NOT account for in this plan was forgetting about Chiller on the cats, which saw Benkei run in first to apply it to Butcher.  I also didn't account for Abyssal Gate, which Tyrus used to teleport my Revenant Champion out of Guard Dog range.  This is something I could have accounted for with better positioning or simply having Constance apply Aegis to it, but I was duly punished for my carelessness.  A Ghast followed by 2 units of Stir The Blood Soulless Blademasters came in at me and finished Butcher off with probably 3 attacks to spare.

Round 4: Kishtaar vs. Vilkul (Winter Korps) on Wolves At Our Heels

A third Donut Holes teammate battle!  This one was an interesting game as Kishtaar and Vilkul are both fairly fragile casters and so it's a very "who blinks first" style of game.  Thus, we kept our distance from each other.  Going second on scenario effectively gave me the first strike, which I used to kill Razor and most of his Shock Trooper units.  His counterattack with the Hounds, Krueger and Gallant was brutal, setting me back a Tyrant, Barragers, and most of my Reavers.  The middle was a trading game with a Tyrant going in to kill Gallant (with help from Silence of Death and Dark Shroud), dying to Connie's vengeance, before finally being brought down by another Tyrant.  Kishtaar put in overtime killing the Hounds and Zaccheaus while Vilkul mostly stood near her own 40mm and was instrumental in bringing down the Execrators and removing models from my scenario terrain with her thrown axes.

Once the Hounds were finally dead, I ran a unit of Witch Coven to my 40mm and finally started accumulating points on it.  Thanks to my contesting models on the left, he wasn't able to follow suit and I ended up scoring the 3 VP "jackpot" of Wolves.  Kishtaar moved up the board laterally keeping her distance from Vilkul and set about ending a turn inside my opponent's scenario forest, killing the scoring Battle Mechanik inside it and the last Shock Trooper Gunner that could possibly contest her now insurmountable scenario lead.

And here's where I screwed up.  Following Kishtaar finishing off any models that could contest her scenario advantage, I decided to protect her by spending her last two focus on Sure Foot.  It was sort of a reactive thing regardless as I had ensured that she was not within Vilkul's 18" melee death range.  I had neglected to consider her 19" walk-Cyclone-throw axes into Stealth death range and her Blessed axes meant I had trade my overboost protection for effectively nothing.  This cost me the game as Vilkul nailed her axe attacks and overkilled me by 5 boxes, snatching victory from the jaws of defeat.  A harsh, but important lesson for me.

Round 5 (Sunday): Butcher vs. Dekathus (Necrofactorium) on Two Fronts

This was an interesting one since Dekathus effectively camped the 50mm side of the field with Hades and a unit of Mechanithrall Brutes, while the rest of his troops swarmed the 40mm side.  I went second and took as scenario terrain the rubble in the middle. I got an early lead bottom of 2 with my Redlined Harpoon Tyrant able to drag in Hades and then finish it off with my Flail Tyrant, but my attempts to wipe out a unit of Criterions with my Rhoks and Assault Reavers ended in failure and my opponent was very fastidious in not giving Butcher any easy charge targets around the obstruction he was cagily moving around.

My opportunity came from the true MVP of the game, the Harpoon Tyrant, who managed to find and pull in a Criterion in the other unit without killing it.  This game Butcher the charge target he needed to get distance, surf into a nearby Night Terror behind a wall, and from there into the rest of his troops, racking up a brutal 14 model kill count and talking total control of the 40mm objectives.

Credit: Tried & True

Dekathus and the Brute Thralls eventually committed and, over the course of two turns, they were able to kill Gallant, but stopped short of finishing off Constance.  By then, there was simply no more material to contest with and I scored the most army points of any game I would play that weekend.

I did decide to drop out at this point to avoid undue pressure related to making my flight home at the end of the event.  I did get to witness some of the final games played, including the final match between Grymkin and Convergence that ultimately ended in a Grymkin victory.  Congratulations to Cody Demunn for piloting Old Witch to a perfect record over 6 grueling rounds.

Saturday: NOVA Warmachine Team Tournament

Longshanks here.

Round 1: Butcher vs. Craghorn (Kithguard) on Trench Warfare

Our opening round into Team Absolute Destruction had me take on a pairing I had a fairly fresh experience into, although this Craghorn list was notably different from the Thursday night one.  He traded Ramhead and the weapon crews for Klangor, Chomper and the Scrappers and played very aggressively by comparison to my last Craghorn game.

His turn 2 Feat and Ambushes saw Chomper emerge to take out Gallant while the Scrappers and Steelbacks went for my Rhoks and front line jacks.  His Sidewinder and Kithguard infantry played defense for his other objectives.  The Scrappers didn't deal much damage through my Shield Guards though (since the Shield Guard models were outside Sneak Attack range) and my counterattack with Butcher had him kill all the Scrappers and 2 Steelbacks, while the feat tokens enabled my Tyrants and other Rhok unit to kill Klangor and Chomper.  Constance counterattacked into a few Kithguard infantry before being shot down and my Harpoon Tyrant that helped kill Chomper managed to hold the line and avoid being shot down by the Throat Cutters long enough that I could secure the right side 50mm indefinitely and start moving troops into taking his 40mm once I removed the Guard Tower and Tunnel Rats.  In the end, despite the early gambit to remove Gallant, he didn't have enough gas in the tank to play out the attrition game.

Round 2: Kishtaar vs. Vorsalys (Fane of Nyrro) on Payload

We received the pair-up into Peyton's Make-A-Wish foundation, who ultimately took 3rd, where I played against the titular team captain, rocking an army of vampires and sporting a count's cape to let you know this was serious business

Pictured: Serious Business.  Credit: Tried & True, used with Peyton's permission

I did have some innate advantages here as the scenario was Payload and I forced Peyton to go second, meaning that his opportunity to generate pre-conflict Dominion hunger was limited and my Arcane Vortex protection was total.  I feated top of 2 and was able to Ricochet off Gallant to kill Merciless in order to trigger Hell Hunters to ensure all 3 Tyrants had valuable targets for their Quad-Bolters.  Peyton had expected me to remove Sybaris from the table (it was behind cover that was no defense against my Hunter Tyrant), but also lost the Strygon and two Klyveneesh as well as a handful of Merciless in the bargain, though my attempts to chip damage Gallant mostly ended in failure.

Vorsalys' feat counterattack so him fearlessly go up to his 40mm, though he couldn't quite clear all the Assault Reavers off the point.  Most of the rest of the Merciless were killed by Last Words, but they cleared the way for Constance to take out the Execrator unit, which in turn left Gallant and his Strygon Rider able to charge and kill one of my Tyrants and damage enough, with a healthy application of Blinding Light on various places.

It was here Peyton made a critical error: He failed to reposition Gallant back within 3" of Constance.  At only one focus and Weakened after killing the Execrators, Kishtaar easily dispatched her and my remaining Tyrants (one Blinded, but with the Shredder melee weapon) killing the Strygon Rider and the last Klyvenesh.  With very little material left, Peyton went for an assassination on Kishtaar, using Perdition to get within range where he could blast her with multiple Blinding Lights.  Thanks to some poor dice, he needed to spend more fury than anticipated to get range on Kishtaar, giving him 3 spells worth of boosted POW 10 damage roles into a 1 focus Kishtaar with Sure Foot.  It was a close thing, but the final spell, with Vorsalys' final fury point earmarked for damage, rolled snake eyes.  The loss didn't hurt Peyton's team much, as they took the round, but it was an excellent matchup into a situation where I felt initially like I had every advantage and turned into a close game despite some errors.  Fane are certainly a force to be reckoned with.

Round 3: Butcher vs. Mordikaar (Exalted) on High Stakes

This team matchup was the Donut Holes vs the Molke Princess Posse.  I'm told this team matchup carries some significance for Dungeon Crawler Carl fans.

By fortune, I got another stream table match, and this one painted Butcher in a much more flattering light.  He took incredibly defensive approaches controlling his side objectives while Butcher threatened to get to his 40mm if he was careless.  There was an obstruction right next to the 50mm that essentially allowed both of us to contest the 50mm from near-perfect safety and each of us were waiting for the other to make the first move.  I took that advantage, finding an angle where my Harpoon Tyrant could drag his Titan Gladiator into range of my other heavies, though I had to commit both Gallant and my Flail Tyrant to finish it off.  He responded by sending in his Aradus Soldier to kill the Harpoon Tyrant and flooding the center with feated Immortals.

My Tyrant was able to clear out by Trampling away, managing to kill the one Immortal actually engaging Gallant and freeing him up to charge and deal some damage to the Soldier.  Most importantly, this freed up space for Butcher to land in the middle of the tightly-packed Exalted army.  It was a little nerve-wracking as I mostly needed 6s to hit the targets there between the Feat, the Extoller UAs, and the Swarm Soldier and only 1 reroll into Poltergeist meant I had very little margin for error, but the dice did not fail me.  Butcher carved an unstoppable swathe of destruction through the middle of the board, culminating in killing Aberration in 3 hits (including Vision) and ending the turn with 14 Blood-Quenched stacks.  It's weird that it happened twice.

Before... Credit: The Ice King ...and after. Credit: The Ice King

Mordikaar's insult-to-injury continued when he failed to hit my Rhok Harrier with a boosted spray, leaving him unable to Void Walk to safety.  Although Butcher got Paralyzed by the Krea, he simply walked up to it and killed it, carved through a couple of Paingivers, and then 2-shot Mordikaar for the win.  Certainly got to put on a show for the stream and end on a high note as the team defeated the Princess Posse (though still ended below them in the final standings based on individual game wins).

Final Thoughts

So, what does this say about Sea Raiders as we approach the terminus of the gaming season for the year?  I think that they're in a fairly competitive place.  They certainly have weaknesses (I was happy that I didn't have to face the likes of Caine or Rosko), but they can play into a wide variety of matchups, have some neat tricks and dark horse factors that might surprise opponents ("Kishtaar's feat lasts a ROUND?") and, in the case of Butcher blowing through whole armies by himself, are simply just fun to play.  I've heard it said that Sea Raiders are on SFG's list for some form of rework to give them a greater faction identity, and while I look forward to that, I hope they understand that between all the tricks and unique mechanics, that a pure stats army can be fun, good for the game, and a good entry recommendation for newer players who want to run the original conquerors of the Iron Kingdoms.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: [Kill Team] Tactical Focus: Raveners
content:
This series of Kill Team articles we take a deep dive into one of the available teams, analyzing each team's strengths and weaknesses, how to set up important plays, and ultimately what to consider to pilot the team to victory. Note that this article assumes you already have knowledge of the basic rules for each team, and will reference abilities and ploys from that team throughout. If you want to learn more about the rules for each team, you can find the most up to date version of the rules on the Warhammer Community Website here. In this article, we’re covering Raveners, the terror from below. 

Kill Team’s first and only bespoke Tyranid team, the Hyperadapted Raveners are the Hive Mind's answer to particularly stubborn defenders of would-be biomass. Genetically modified from the typical Ravener strain encountered by the empires and war bands of the galaxy, these subterranean super predators are equipped with chameleonic skin, steel-melting venom, and the sinister alien intelligence required to operate far from the Synapse creatures of a Tyranid vanguard. These biological adaptations are well reflected in their game rules, and Ravener players have many tools at their disposal to subsume their enemies into piles of biological refuse.

Basic Overview

In keeping with the fine tradition of Raveners menacing unsuspecting ground walkers, their primary rule involves creating a Tunnel that will creep across the Killzone as the game proceeds. Raveners can Burrow into and out of this Tunnel for 1AP, striking from below quickly or avoiding the wrath of enemy operatives by leaving the Killzone. Playing around your Tunnel is also how you get the most out of your Ploys, as almost all of them revolve around it in some capacity. Offensive ploys like Death From Below and Burrowing Strike can provide that extra kick you need to finish off tough enemies in a timely manner, while defensive ploys such as Whipchord Emergence and Writhe Out Of Sight can keep your limited retinue of operatives alive. 

Their other faction rule, Predatory Instincts, allows them to perform two Fight actions per activation, as well as counteract regardless of their order. Raveners can change their order before they counteract, or swap their order as a counteraction. This allows you to change your Engage order to a Conceal, or vice versa, and with clever positioning you can incapacitate enemy operatives on counteractions by swapping to Conceal before Fighting, preventing your enemy from returning fire without further exposing themselves. 

Finally, during their counteraction, Raveners can perform a free Burrow action, as long as they aren’t performing Mission Actions during that counteraction. This can be done before or after their normal action, and in addition to the order swap, allowing you some very effective ways to eliminate the enemy without risking Shoot actions in return. The most important thing to remember here is you cannot do Mission Actions during a counteraction in which you Burrow, so planning ahead is crucial depending on your Crit Op. Missions like Transmission or Loot can leave you at a VP deficit if you aren’t considerate of your limited action economy. 

Team Strengths and Weaknesses

In spite of recent nerfs that have reigned the team’s dominance in a bit, Raveners are still a monstrous menace on the tabletop. Emphasizing hit and run tactics, they are at their best when able to stage multiple threats with both operatives in the Tunnel and the ones above. Unlike almost every other team, Raveners are able to exude an aura of threat around the Tunnel that opponents must be wary of lest their operatives feed the Hive (and your Kill Op.) However, the 5+ save and reduced wounds means the team is still vulnerable to being shot off the board if it overextends, and having a mere five operatives means every Ravener you give up is a point for your opponent. Choosing when to engage your enemy is absolutely paramount to avoid unnecessary chip damage and early losses. 

Your five specialist operatives are all important and superior to the generic Warrior operative, so there is never a reason not to take them. Your leader, the Ravener Prime, provides the Synaptic Link Strategic Gambit, potentially giving you big Command Point bonuses in the first few Turning Points. Besides having the Ravener equivalent of a Chainsword (5A 3+ ⅘) with the Rending weapon rule, it also lowers the APL of nearby enemy operatives contesting objective markers, allowing you snatch markers away from your opponents on a crucial objective. Finally, the Prime also turns off your opponents rerolls within 3”, meaning anyone the Prime fights, or anyone foolish enough to Charge or get close enough Shoot it on conceal, is entirely at the whim of fate for any rolls that they make. 

A Ravener Prime rears up before striking at bloodthirsty heretics. Credit: Laura Marshall

Your only ranged piece, the Venomspitter, is a real game changer. While many players prefer utilizing it as a defensive piece, which it does excel at, the Venomspitter can also be used as a mobile weapons platform. Lacking the Heavy keyword on its dangerous weapon profile means the Venomspitter can easily Burrow into the Killzone, Reposition, and take a key Shoot at a specific operative with the Focused profile, or a clustered enemy group with the Blast profile. If an opponent moves too close to the tunnel, you can Burrow, Distend Dorsal Sac, and take an even more devastating Shoot at would be aggressors. Don’t be afraid to use it in a Fight either, as it still maintains the Ravener Chainsword profile every other operative has. 

Your remaining three operatives all have their use cases as well. The Tremorscythe stays in the Tunnel, deterring anybody from approaching your ever expanding territory lest their activation be interrupted. When it comes time for it to emerge, the ability to Charge on Conceal can save you headaches from being shot later on. Keep in mind this operative doesn’t have to Fight when it interrupts; a well-placed Krak grenade can be more beneficial at times. The Felltalon’s awesome melee profile, boasting Lethal 5+, Shock, and Poison, makes short work of even the toughest combatants, and it has the ability to soften them up with his Toxic Lunge, dealing wounds directly. A 6” Silent Poison shooting weapon gives it some ranged utility during your counteractions as well. Finally, the Wrecker boasts a 4+ save, reduces incoming damage, and the Crush rule on his melee weapon allows for game swinging damage spikes if you roll well. Don’t forget this operative’s 3” Silent ranged tail weapon, which all the Raveners come equipped with, also has the Piercing 1 rule. 

It’s not all sunshine and biomass here though. As mentioned, the 5+ Save most of your operatives have leave them very vulnerable to Shoot actions. With the change to their Wounds stat, the Ravener dreads the melta gun even more than before. Previously, even four hits was survivable with the single saving throw afforded by the melta, but this is no longer the case except on your Ravener Prime. Four hits guarantees death for these beasts, so be mindful of where your opponent is staging their melta Gunner. If you have an opportunity to take it out, do so, but baiting the melta into moving up and taking a shot in a place where you can eliminate him afterward can be a valid, if risky, tactic. While the melta is certainly the deadliest threat to your operatives, all shooting is potentially lethal to you, so be careful which shots you allow your opponent to take. 

Outside of combat, Raveners struggle heavily with their action economy. With just 15 AP across your five activations, and Burrow costing an AP reducing this action economy even further, you may suffer from indecision regarding where to commit your operatives. You’ll find certain Crit Ops, like Loot or Data, to be difficult to play, as you may have to commit an entire operative to playing the Crit Op, and potentially being dead in the water. Every action on every activation matters. Whether or not you’re able to manage these decisions effectively will determine a huge portion of your success.  

Raveners are at their best around the Tunnel, and even more vulnerable away from it. Overextending early to take suboptimal fights can spell doom for you if not done in a calculated manner. If you do have to move far from the Tunnel, try and remember the 7” Rule. The Tunnel moves 5”, and Writhe Out Of Sight is usable on an operative within 2”. Any Ravener within 7” of the previous Tunnel marker is potentially saveable with this combo. A Ravener alive at one or two wounds is a Ravener that isn’t contributing to your opponent's Kill Op score. 

Standout Tactics

If the Ravener stat line is the hammer, the faction rules and Firefight Ploys are the scalpel. With several sources of mortal damage, ways to escape combat or reposition for a more optimal Fight, and the ability to Burrow directly into control range, Raveners are perfectly poised for an ambush predator style of gameplay.

Let’s start with the Tunnel and Burrow. While you should have a general idea of where your tunnel wants to go, always stay flexible with it and be ready to adjust the plan as necessary. Making a pivot in Turning Point 3 or 4 to keep a piece alive can be more important than strictly adhering to whatever plan you might have had for the Tunnel, especially if you lose the initiative roll. Writhe Out Of Sight is easily your most important survival tool and can get you out of many difficult situations. On the opposite side, winning the initiative can let you position your tunnel into an opportunistic angle, where you can possibly Burrow into control range of two or more enemy operatives, hitting them all with the mortal damage from the Burrowing Strike Firefight Ploy, before performing two Fight actions and incapacitating them both. In these situations, be sure to decide which operative is the greater threat in a Fight, and whether or not you want to deal with the weaker one first to deny combat assistance. A clever Charge can also leave you poised to Burrow away after the Fight. Keep in mind you can Burrow both into and out of control range, so if a Fight doesn’t go your way, you have a way to escape.

Another deadly tool in your arsenal is the Slithering Evasion Firefight Ploy. This lets you Fall Back for a single AP, but more importantly, it can let you Charge out of control range. If your opponent overextends an operative in a Turning Point, this can allow you to stage multiple models off your opponents. When you’re ready, one operative can Charge away into two others, incapacitating them while the other stays on the original enemy model, ready to incapacitate him before Charging elsewhere. Keep an eye out for these emergent opportunities as seizing them will be critical.

The Venomspitter can be a key piece in removing enemy models On Guard in Close Quarters Killzones. This model's head tends to overhang its base, meaning it can draw line of sight from some weird angles. Since models On Guard tend to only see in a specific direction, while simultaneously exposing parts of their own model, the Venomspitter can very easily set up and deal with these pesky operatives in a way that doesn’t allow the enemy to return fire.

I see you; you don't see me.

A final nasty trick in your repertoire should be an understanding of how to make counteractions work in your favor. Raveners are currently one of three teams that can perform multiple actions on counteractions, performing a free Burrow and an additional action. Normally during an activation, operatives are limited to performing any given action a single time, but counteractions don’t have this action limit imposed on them. While the other two teams that can do this, Deathwatch and Angels of Death, both specify that during a counteraction their actions must be different, Raveners do not have this stipulation. What this means is an operative can Burrow for free, and then Burrow for 1AP, performing the Burrowing Strike Firefight Ploy between them. While a niche use case, dealing 2-4 mortal wounds to enemy operative or operatives without risking anything in return in terms of damage is an excellent trick to have in your back pocket should the opportunity arise, whether you use it to finish off an enemy or merely weaken one for the future.

Your equipment selection is going to be more flexible than most other teams, as Raveners don’t have much in the way of mandatory considerations. That said, Metamorphic Flesh is something you want to take almost every game as the healing it provides is indispensable. Chromatospore Camouflage is something to consider, but always clarify with your opponent how much access to Saturate they have. If the enemy has a lot of weapons with the rule, it won’t be doing anything for you. Acid Blood is something to consider in the Elite match up, as the extra mortal damage can make or break a fight for you (just remember that you have it, as it can be easy to forget about.) Heightened Senses is probably something you can leave behind, but if you’re struggling to fill out a fourth slot, it can give you an edge in a key initiative roll. Light Barricades are unnecessary thanks to the Tunnel Lurkers strategy ploy providing cover on your Tunnel. Krak Grenades are something to consider in the Elite match up as well, giving your ranged attacks a bit of extra spice.

Tac Ops and Crit Ops

Raveners archetypes of Seek & Destroy and Infiltration presently occupy a weird position in the game. In the Seek & Destroy category, Route involves a risky overextension in Turning Point 2 if you want to maximize your score. Sweep and Clear has the same problem as Route, while further straining your action economy with extraneous mission actions. On the Infiltration side of things, Track Enemy involves a lot of assumption your opponent will be giving valid targets for your operatives early, and that you yourself won’t be for them, which isn’t really what the team wants to be doing. Plant Devices has the same issues as Sweep and Clear, bogging your team down with unnecessary mission actions and risking exposure. Steal Intelligence also requires early exposure, and performing wasteful Pick Up Marker actions when you could be making Fights or playing Crit Op.

By far the best choice for tac op, even with recent changes, remains Dominate. There are no extra actions required, it rewards you doing what you want to be doing anyway (slaughtering your opponents operatives), but perhaps most importantly, it isn’t scoreable until Turning Point 3, which as we’ll discuss is when the Raveners game should truly be starting. Keep in mind you can still Burrow while having Dominate tokens, you just won’t be able to collect them. This can be useful Turning Point 3 to keep an operative alive until Turning Point 4, when it comes time to collect them. 

For Crit Ops, Raveners best ones are things that don’t require them to be wasting valuable AP. Things like Loot and Download where you can set up to get your point early, or force your opponent to do so, expending an operative in the process, are going to be some of their easier missions to play. Transmission, Stake Claim, Reboot, and Data can force you to leave an operative behind if you don’t wish to fall too behind on VP. A defensive tunnel can come in handy here in case operatives need to do rapid shifting around. Orb and Energy Cells are some of the hardest missions for the team to play. You can pick up an Energy Cell early in the game, but the operative who does so now needs to choose between staying safe the remainder of the game, or going towards the enemy and risking bringing their marker towards them. In this case, and especially for Orb, an offensive tunnel where your opponent is forced to play around their own objectives can be very handy. 

Matchup Considerations

With their high movement, wounds, and chainsword equivalents, Raveners enjoy a healthy range of favorable match ups. Most 7W or 8W teams are going to be trying to stay a reasonable distance from your operatives and your Tunnel to avoid being made mincemeat out of, but even this can only delay things for so long. Teams like Death Korp, Brood Brothers, Aquilons, and Spectre Squad are all going to try using their hard hitting melta and general ranged shenanigans to whittle you down. Patience will pay off in these ranged match ups, as eventually these teams have to extend to play the game they want to play. When they do, Raveners get to play the game they want to play.

Elf teams (Corsairs, Blades of Khaine, Hand of the Archon, and Mandrakes) are some of the best match ups you might encounter. With their 8W making them ripe for the picking, Elf teams will struggle heavily into Raveners if you’re playing a careful game. Mandrakes in particular deserve a special shout out, as they are currently the only team in the game that actually improves Raveners Save Stat, as Soul Strike is not an optional rule at the time of this writing. That doesn’t mean you can allow these teams to shoot you at will though. The plan remains the same into these teams, the execution (of your enemy) just becomes a bit easier in Fights.

Deathwatch can present a unique problem. The Deathwatch Gunner Veteran operative is the bane of Raveners, and with Suffer Not The Alien and applying Devastating Wounds to the weapon, the Gunner can easily incapacitate two operatives before you’re able to put him down. Be cautious of this operative, and the team in general. The reduction to 18W means power weapons can potentially kill your operatives with three critical successes before you’re able to kill them. You must be especially patient with Deathwatch, and only make trades when they are favorable to you.

Sanctifiers can also present a problem to the team. While ostensibly a 7W team, there are a few operatives with 8W, and more importantly, their Ministorum Sermon faction rule can make your scything talons feel a bit anemic. Furthermore, many of their weapons have Saturate on them, meaning your Chromatospore Camouflage equipment is not a reliable option here. To top it all off, they also have access to a melta gun themselves. Be extremely cautious in this match up. Try to use the Venomspitter, Felltalon, and Burrowing Strike to deal mortal wounds to ensure you’re killing them in one or two hits. No single operative on this team is going to kill a Ravener in a single fight, but losing out on a critical hit and taking two hits instead of one multiple times can cause you to take more chip damage than is sustainable for you long term.

Piloting the Team to Victory

The Tunnel being such a key part of the team makes us ask the question: just where does it go? Generally speaking, the Tunnel can be used in an offensive or defensive fashion. A defensive Tunnel wants to thread through your home objective marker before making its way towards the center. An offensive Tunnel wants to beeline for the center marker before making its way towards your opponents home objective. What you decide is going to depend on your opponent, the Crit Op, and the Killzone. If your opponent is playing an aggressive team, staging an offensive Tunnel will allow you to punch them much harder than they punch you, as well providing egress when your operatives need to retreat. By the same token, a cagey or defensive team allows you to play a defensive Tunnel yourself, and punish any enemy operative who wanders away from the relative safety of your opponents back line.

A critical thing to your success here is using the right piece for the job. Your Ravener Prime might want to occupy the center point to seize it away from your opponent with its APL manipulation. Sometimes the Felltalon needs to go in to wither down a particularly stubborn enemy operative, like the Deathwatch Demolisher who reduces incoming damage. These kinds of operatives are especially susceptible to both the mortal wounds Toxic Lunge inflicts, as well as the Poison it leaves behind.

Raveners real game begins on Turning Point 3. By this point, the Tunnel should be either already on or reaching the center objective, and enemy operatives will be in position to be charged directly out of the Tunnel. Positioning your third Tunnel marker to charge multiple operatives will be a key factor in your success, and you should be aiming to take away as many activations from your opponent as is possible. Fewer activations means fewer opportunities for something to go wrong for your own operatives, as well as giving your opponent less time and actions to play their own game. Raveners are performing a balancing act with this: the more your total APL can outweigh your opponents total APL, and the faster this can be tipped in your favor, the better.

A Brood Brother realizes just how expendable he is to the Star Gods. Credit: Laura Marshall

Final Thoughts

A team that requires more patience than most, Raveners should always be walking the line between caution and aggression. You’ve likely read the word “opportunity” a lot in this article, and while spotting these things is a key part of playing Kill Team in general, it is even more important with this ambush team. Embrace the Ravener mindset, and think like a predator, always waiting for your opponent to make that mistake that will cost them the game. Strike too soon, your operatives will be lost to volleys of shooting attacks. Wait too long, your opponent will run away on VP before you have a chance. Timing is absolutely key, and knowing when to strike will be the difference between your Tunnel collapsing on itself, or dragging your opponent into the sandy depths.

Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: Historicals: SAGA Age of Invasions FAQ 2026
content:
There’s clearly something in the air over at Studio Tomahawk - hot on the heels of a new FAQ and rework of Age of Vikings comes one for Age of Invasions. That’s particularly exciting as Age of Invasions has legendarily gone un-FAQ’d since release, possibly because it was blessed by Constantine and possibly because Studio Tomahawk just didn’t get around to it. There’s nothing in here on the level of the near complete rework the Irish board got in Age of Vikings, but some big changes for popular factions are sure to put the barbarians among the limitanei, so let’s dive in for a look.

Clarifications and FAQs

There’s a couple of clarifications to core rules and equipment that bring Age of Invasions in line with other, faq’d, SAGA ages. Elephants in units of two (you mad bastard) now do 4, (or 8 vs units that have closed ranks or are mounted on horses) automatic hits on the charge. This was clear in other books that were heavier on the elephants, so your elephants are not getting worse with age and hit just as hard now as they did in the Age of Caesars. Elephant fans will also rejoice that the manubalista hits them with a paltry aggression of 1, proving that the Romans literally couldn’t hit an elephant at this distance. Combined with a couple of the battle board changes, the few elephants we see in Age of Invasions are confirmed to be deadly and hard to remove.

ELEPHANTS. Age of Invasions is a great excuse to slap some powerful pachyderms on the tabletop, as this Sassanid war elephant shows. (Credit - author's collection)

There are some possibly needed clarifications to how Heroic Units work with regards to the Britons board. I’ve played a couple of games against people using this in all sorts of ways, so it’s good to have it nailed down:

  • Warlords in Heroic Units can have a Banner
  • Heroic Units with the Warlord will not count as galvanised even though they’re within range (there’s at least one game I can think of where this would have made a big difference!)
  • You cannot use Bodyguards until all the Heroes are dead (no sacrificing a hearthguard to save a companion)
  • We Obey is measured from any point in the Heroic Unit
I think this comes out fairly even as - I think! - most people were playing with more or less these rules. If you were one of the few who had permanently galvanised Companions in a unit with the Warlord you were playing it wrong anyway!

The biggest clarification is also one of the most obvious - you cannot use the fatigues of a Goth unit activated with Resolve to cancel their activation. The entire and obvious point of the ability was to let you charge with two fatigues, so having this plainly said is much appreciated by all tired Goth lovers everywhere.  

Mercenaries

A few minor clarifications to Mercenaries make for very little change as, beyond the Personal Champion accompanying a Chariot-mounted Warlord having a horse and javelins (not a chariot), these were all clear.

Guides have been clarified to work with Tournament scenarios, guaranteeing their extra terrain placement, and the rules have been clarified. 

Every box should have a dog in it. Barons' War Command, Wargames Atlantic

The Molossians can no longer close ranks, which makes sense, because they’re just eight dogs.

Faction Changes

Three changes that will turn up frequently, and one that no one will notice.

First off, the Romans get to take TWO manuballistae, which immediately struck fear into the heart of everyone who takes large units of cavalry. As a reminder, the manuballista is a 2xL special shooting attack that rolls half as many dice as models in the target unit, and is therefore terrifying. It’s still a unit of levies, so you can’t use Combined Formation on them, but Barritus and In This Sign, Conquer, are still up for grabs.

Wait, Fuck, that's not the right kind of Ballistarii
Credit: Pendulin Briton Companions are clearer, with their own unit profile (identical to the Hearthguard), and can’t be galvanised, but other than that there are no real changes. It all reads better though, which is good. 

Frankish Franciscas can now be equipped by Loyal Mercenaries, which will make for some fun axe throwing Bishops. Franciscas power up some of the main offensive Frankish abilities, so you could plausibly end up with a Bishop who is incredibly good on the charge, but more likely you’re using this to beef up a Personal Champion, who goes from an interesting pick to a very good one with the Frankish board.

The one no one will notice is Theoderic, King of the Visigoths, has got a little bit choppier, as instead of getting bonus dice he just receives additional aggression for each fatigue. Unfortunately, you almost never see legendary units on the table!   

Battle Board Changes

Saxons

A unit of Late Anglo-Saxon warriors. Credit: Eric Lofgren, painting by Nevermore Painting Studios.

Two changes for the Saxons that amount to a small buff. Ferocious has had it’s downside removed, as previously you’d exchange 3 attack dice for the loss of a defence dice. This was pretty poor, unless you were beating up levy, so the new version is much improved. Now, you get the three dice (in every melee in the turn), and the first time you win you power up Furor, letting you situationally clear off fatigue. Furor is still risky, but improving dice economy is always a good thing. 

A substantial change to Jeers as well, where previously you’d hoped for a ranged unit to kill 6 of your levy, leading to a situation where you were hoping to fail defence rolls. Instead, the new version boosts your defence against shooting and fatigues the enemy if they fail to remove a model. Matches the idea of jeering your enemy’s paltry shooting much better than the old version!

Britons

Britons have changes to three abilities and one outright replacement.

Hold the Line! Is entirely gone, so you can’t increase the armour of most of your army anymore at the cost of an uncommon and a rare. Good riddance, because that was the leading cause of the Briton Clump, the second most annoying thing about SAGA. The replacement, Forced March, might actually let Briton players move around the board in more than one big pile, as it allows a Hero and up to 2 units to galvanise and move S - not much of a move, and takes an activation, but allows you to galvanise whoever you like for only one common dice. 

Pendragon became more flexible, giving you the choice of both prior effects (or both for the cost of a rare). It’s very good in the rare form, removing fatigue in melee and allowing you to reroll attack dice, but also then works as a situational fatigue removal or attack boost if you need it. Working on your heroes only, this is clearly designed to be an every-turn ability for a Heroic Warlord unit. 

Tenacious can now cost a common, so you’ll put dice on it every time - gaining two defence dice and cancelling a casualty is incredibly good, particularly when you can galvanise much easier now.

The new Shieldwall functions as a bubble of light cover based on a hero, providing light cover to all galvanised units.

Franks

Franks were clearly doing okay, as changes here are fairly small. Momentum now no longer works on Mercenaries, and to be honest, you’re lucky it did in the first place, Clovis. Determination and +1 attack dice is still fantastic. Meanwhile, the Frankish People is clarified to be targeting a single hero, rather than just 3 units around some heroes somewhere.

Goths

Pleasantly for me, as I’m playing Goths in an event in a few weeks, there’s little change here. What change there is is a minor nerf, as Gratia now only provides +1 to defence dice if your unit is on foot. It was too good on Cataphracts, but if they’d waited a few weeks to update it I’d have had mathematical proof it was. Ah well.

Victrix Islamic Horse Archers because we don't have any pictures of Huns - credit Bair

Huns

Bair continually suggests he’s going to build and play Huns, but he’s yet to do it, so I feel good about these changes happening before he has a chance to beat me with them.

Two small nerfs to Hun abilities. Panic has been changed to remove the dice recycling ability, which is good news for Hun enemies as it’s a dice hungry board. The Endless Horde also receives a hit, with the same no fatigue, three unit movement activation remaining, but ruling out any further shooting from those units. It’s now something you’re using to get away from your enemies rather than to spool up the composite bow machine gun.

Picts

Some significant changes here aimed at getting you moving and attacking rather than sitting in solid cover waiting for a reluctant enemy charge.

On that theme, Scouts receives some clearer wording but remains unchanged, letting you zip about the board with ease, while Feint now only works as the attacker. Stalking also gets a bit of a hit, as the ability to sit next to dangerous terrain has been removed - uneven terrain only.

Masters of the Field changes substantially. You’re still picking a terrain piece and getting a benefit for being within it, but now you’re getting additional defence dice instead of solid cover. Ignoring the movement penalty has been shifted to a rare dice effect. Not sure if this is a sidegrade or a significant change, but units in uneven, solid cover, terrain will only benefit.

Romans

Wargames Atlantic Goth Warriors and Victrix Unarmoured Late Romans in comparison. Credit: Lupe

You no longer need an advanced course in logical reasoning to use Combined Formation, as it’s now very, very clear. 

Sassanids

A swathe of changes for the Sassanids that pushes them away from taking all composite bow warriors (take Huns!) or all bow Levy, putting some serious weight behind Elephant and Heathguard units instead. 

We ALSO only have one picture of Sassanids and I've already used it in this article. Saracen horse archers can be deadly. Credit - Ne Cede Malis

Ahriman’s Curse has been nerfed to only give the previously rare dice effect, cancelling cover for a unit being shot at. Still useful, and goes to a common or uncommon dice. 

That’s handy because you’ll want to use a rare dice on Second Wind, which now removes two fatigues from an Elephant or unit without ranged weapons on a rare dice, while retaining common and uncommon single fatigue removal.

Inexorable Advance sees a huge change, with the previous casualty causing effect gone altogether. Now you’re using any dice to inflict fatigue on a unit within S of a single activated Cataphract or Elephant unit, with a rare dice making these activations fatigue free. Less complicated than previous, but potentially much less impactful. Inflicting fatigue is useful, doing so with a fatigue free move is useful, but with good positioning you could chip away at enemy units for a common dice in the previous incarnation.

Armoured is now an activation ability, giving you another (albeit expensive) way to activate for a charge. The effects remain the same but are (handily!) taken out of the melee SAGA ability chain.

Volley fire looks like it’s changed a lot, but as helpfully pointed out to me it ends up doing what it was supposed to be doing in the first place. Instead of gaining bows and determination, a composite bow unit increases its range by M. The results are still shooting L, but now without determination you’re going to have to use a dice to activate them.

Overall

I know you’re thinking this all looks pretty good, but what does it mean for me, Justinian, Emperor of Rome?

All told the changes here aren’t as enormous as in some of the other SAGA age FAQs, but there’s still a shakeup coming. Most of that shakeup is that if you haven’t painted a Personal Champion yet, you really should. A lot of boards just got better for it, and if you’re without one in the Franks and Britons particularly, you should get on it now. Footsore is a good choice, go have fun.

Britons will see a much more interactive playstyle than castling up and slowly walking across the field with armour 5, and might even see some serious use out of Personal Champions and Companions as heroes able to galvanise outflung units. This is a fantastic change, even if the battle board is much the same, as it will let Briton players have fun with things like “movement” that they haven’t utilised before.

It’s likely that you’re celebrating as a Roman player just on the strength of gaining another manuballista and mourning your old list as a Sassanid, so if your plan was to shore up a shaky claim to the purple with a jaunt to the Euphrates, you’re in luck. If you did go all in on composite bows for the Sassanids, the new board will force a different playstyle, where elephants and cataphracts are your main damage dealers - they’re a little easier to clear fatigue off and hit just as hard as ever. It might all end up as a slightly weaker Sassanid board, but to see if that’s true we’ll have to get out there and play!

title: Mayday, Miss Marcy! Pushy Player, Custom Chaos, Party Plateau
content:
Welcome back everyone once again to the advice column you all love to read and read to love, or something like that! That's right, it is once again that time of the week for Mayday, Miss Marcy, in which I take your carefully submitted questions and provide them with carefully considered answers. If you've never joined us here at MMM before, this is a column in the vein of Agony Aunt style reader submitted newspaper articles, and each week I take 3 questions (usually in chronological order!) submitted to me and provide the best answer I can give from my limited perspective and information. If you'd like to have your own questions answered in this very column, read the little blurb below to find out how!

Have a question you want answered on just about anything you’d need advice on in this grand hobby space of ours? Board games, 40k, AOS, TTRPGs, MTG, anything and everything that we cover, we can help with!

For some examples, take a look at previous editions of our column at this link with a handy tag to see all previous questions and answers!

If you want to submit questions, we have a few ways you can do it. Patrons can use the Discord bot command to ask questions, which will be received anonymously!

If you’re not a Patron, or just don’t want extra steps, you can comment on this article, or e-mail me directly at marcy@tabletopbattles.com!

Last week, we had a few questions regarding falling out of the hobby and more, and this week, I once again have a new selection of questions!

Pushing Your Luck

Hi Miss Marcy,

I recently got into the hobby as a player, and I've been having a great time with it. I went from what I assume is the usual path of watching a lot of videos, buying a lot of things, and never doing anything with it to finally painting and playing at a store somewhat near me. I've had some fun so far and the game really is worth all of the other things, but I have an odd problem: one of the players in the store is extremely pushy for my time. Like, they literally ask me almost every day if I'm coming to play or when I will next be at the store, and if I want to play with them. At first I thought this was cool and even how things might want to go, because it meant I'd always have games, but after about a month and a half I am starting to get a little weary. They aren't a bad sport, they are friendly, but it feels a little suffocating to have my game time attached at the hip to this person. I am a little unsure if I should tell them to back off, try to distance myself from them, or just enjoy the fact that I apparently will always have a play partner available to play against. Also, I will provide the following since I see you get a lot of answers without details: we are fairly matched, they don't play unfairly or take advantage of my being new, I do get some other games in sometimes, and we are not attracted to one another (or at least they are not into me that way).

Pushing Off

Dear Pushing,

Okay, first, I love that you've provided me with the details at the end, because it really does help provide the answer. I think, ironically, you didn't provide me something that would help with some of this puzzle: how new is this player comparable to yourself? Because I think my first thought is they are similar to you, a new player who is afraid that their leap into the hobby could be a waste of time if they don't get to play, and they saw a new player like themselves in you. Either way, I think it just sounds like you have a slight mismatch in personalities in that this person is VERY ready to go and excited to play, and you are enjoying yourself but not to the level this person is. I don't really get the sense this person is doing anything wrong, and maybe that's why you aren't approaching it as if they are smothering you, even if it feels like it.

Perhaps I would offer that you are maybe replying too quickly, though. If they are messaging you every day and you are replying immediately, you might be inadvertently setting up the expectation that you WILL answer immediately, which could be creating mixed signals. Either way, I don't know if you really have a problem, just perhaps an issue in which you two are just simply not that into playing the game; to put this another way, I think you are facing the "saying no" problem that sometimes happens in hobbies, in that you feel that saying no is going to torpedo your gaming in general. You can just say no; I assume that you have, at least on days in which you aren't going to play, so it is obvious that saying no is not a problem to them, but it doesn't register to you! So, I'd consider just trying to space out your distance more and see how things go from there. Otherwise, I actually think you might be misreading it as an issue and instead just take the fact that you have a regular, equally matched opponent as a gift!

Custom Made Frustration

Dear Marcy,

I have a problem I've not exactly figured out how to deal with: I play with a player who has a lot of customized units. And by customized, I mean that the models really do not look anything like what they should look like on the surface, and instead are "counts as". This wouldn't be an issue except that they tend to use models with the same base size to stand in for different things, occasionally making it deeply confusing what a unit is actually supposed to be. They will offer the answer to this question, but it really just is not intuitive to know what unit and what weapons something is supposed to have when it is neither WYSIWYG OR even visually close to the model in question. I'm starting to want to not play against them, despite the fact that they are actually a good sport and generally a decent opponent, but it is starting to feel like I'm having to do too much homework to remember what their army is supposed to be on any given day.

Customized

Dear Customized,

I think you really just need to state to them that if they are going to change what models are supposed to represent without having it be visually clear, they need to start doing something to make it clearer for you (and any other opponents) what they are. The onus of work here rests on your opponent, not yourself, and you really putting up with it at all is probably going a bit too far and validating the behavior. I really would recommend you start demanding they provide clarity to what they are playing. Whether that is a printed or documented list, some sort of visualized thing on the models, or even something on the bases, it really just sounds like they are taking the cheapest possible option to using non-standard models to stand-in for various things without actually putting in any real effort to make them "Counts as" beyond simply saying they are. Frankly, your opponent may as well just be playing with blank bases and just telling you one of them is a Captain or something else.

Party's Over

Miss Marcy,

My TTRPG party has been playing together for a few years now, and we're running into a problem that there really just doesn't seem to be much left to do, but players also seem kind of reluctant to let go of the characters they've built up over the course of this campaign. I don't think I'd say anything here is stellar or amazing world building or lore writing, but we always seem to be pushing off from starting something new by continuing the thing we've been doing for a while now. It is so boring that there are times I don't want to go anymore, but it is one of my biggest social outlets and my friend circle, so it does feel pretty bad to give it up. Do you have any suggestions? I realize I am just asking for creative ways to get my party to do something else, because I haven't come up with anything.

Partied Out

Dear Partied Out,

Okay, let's just get down to it: your players don't really care about the TTRPG, they care about hanging out and playing a game, a game in which they roll some dice and likely kill some stuff, maybe they do some jokes or bits, and then they go home. If you've been running a campaign this long that hasn't presented anything that scales high to present any real challenge, you aren't really role playing anymore, you all are just playing combat simulator. Which, if you're playing Dungeons and Dragons, is actually the correct end game of the entire process. Otherwise, I think as far as ideas, you are going to need to start presenting things as a need to refresh. Why not have your players consider what the next generation of the cast would be? Or try a new system and have them transport their characters to it, but help reset the power levels somehow. I can understand change being scary, but if you aren't having fun, you either need to convince the group to do something new, or find something else to do. It may not even be playing a TTRPG; have you all just considered playing board games or something else? Because the 'role' part seems to be pretty absent.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning?
