And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Critical Role Codenames is a far better board game than it has any right to be
content:
Our Verdict

Codenames: Critical Role Adventures is a novel spin on an established classic. Its inventive new mechanics justify its existence without spoiling the elegance of the original board game. It's so approachable, you don't need to follow Critical Role! As long as you're okay with one or two incredibly tough words, you're up to the task of this challenging campaign game.

Pros
  • Inventive new ideas
  • Same classic wordplay
  • Easy and approachable
Cons
  • More expensive than Codenames
  • Limited replayability
  • Higher difficulty

Codenames: Critical Role Adventures is a wonderful board game, but it faces one hell of an uphill battle. Step one: convince the world they don't need to like Critical Role to play. Step two: convince the world to buy a less replayable version of a game they already love that also costs more money. Step three: profit???

It's a tough sell, especially when many will take one glance at the box and write it off as a cash grab. Perhaps it is a cash grab (yay, capitalism!), but designers Vlaada Chvátil and Felix Podlesny have still given it their all. This is an excellent evolution of Chvátil's original Codenames formula.

It's inventive and exciting, and it mostly manages to avoid spoiling the original's simplicity. If you're a Codenames addict, it's a must-have - whether you care about Critical Role or not.

Basically, this is a co-op Codenames campaign. If you know anything at all about Dungeons and Dragons, you can picture it already. Three adventurers must work together to complete quests, grab loot, and advance the story of their adventure. You might even get to roll a D20.

Critical Role Codenames can accommodate much larger player counts (or even smaller), but you always use three characters from Critical Role canon. Each comes with a character sheet and a unique power. Grog the beefy Barbarian gets extra modifiers on D20 rolls if he's taken damage. Dorian the Bard can use songs to prevent damage and farm XP. Fresh Cut Grass…blows up if he gets too stressed?

I've used a lot of terms there that make sense in a D&D game, but not in Codenames. So how does this work, exactly?

You still have your word cards in rows and columns. Instead of Spymasters, you have a single Dungeon Master, who gives one-word, one-number clues as usual. When you think you know what they're getting at, you place a character's standee on the word of your choice.

If the guess was correct, there are two possible outcomes. The DM might place a gold token on top of the word. Congrats! Your guess was right, and you get an XP token as a reward. Generally, you need to discover a specific number of gold tiles to complete a scenario (though the game's three campaigns often bend these rules for variety).

Alternatively, you might discover a Blue token. These are still correct guesses, but they trigger an effect specific to the scenario. They're usually beneficial (though, again, some scenarios experiment). You might pick up money to spend on magic items in a store, or you might earn an extra hint from the DM.

Things can go wrong in plenty of ways, however. Grey and red tokens deal damage to a character, and you fail the mission if someone loses all their HP.

Red tokens also act as timers that count down to mission failure. When you get a wrong answer or choose to stop guessing, the DM places a red token on your grid before a new round begins. Run out of red tokens, and it's game over.

Plus, the dreaded assassin remains in play. This still acts as an insta-death, but Critical Role Codenames gives it a new role, too. As you advance through a campaign's scenarios, you'll encounter boss fights that require you to discover the assassin after meeting your usual guessing goals. It's a thematic and interesting spin on an infamous mechanic.

Critical Role Codenames keeps on innovating by changing things up from scenario to scenario. Win conditions change, and special rules come into play. The actual narrative of the three campaigns is barely there, but I'll forgive Czech Games Edition for not giving Matt-Mercer-worthy descriptions. The campaigns' maps and prologues are all just set dressing - pleasing, but not necessary to enjoy the game.

The campaign structure of this game does hamper its replayability, of course. The original Codenames can be played endlessly. Each of these campaigns does offer branching paths, so there's some reason to return and replay, but you don't miss much by sticking to a single path. All roads on the map lead to the same outcome, story-wise.

It's also worth mentioning the increase in difficulty. Some of these scenarios are absolutely brutal. Without spoiling anything, there are one or two where you should expect to fail repeatedly - the clues and time you get are that sparse.

The word cards up this difficulty further. While CGE has saved its most specific Easter Eggs for the Vox Machina expansion, there are still some words here that make no sense outside a Critical Role context.

What kind of clues would you give for 'Exandria', 'Plainscow', 'Briarwood', and 'Earthbreaker'? What the hell is an Unseen Servant, or a Red Moon? What is 'The List' referring to? Even if you do get these references, they're tough to chain to other, more generic words with a single clue.

Okay, so this game isn't perfect for a non-Critter. Those words are easily removed, though, and the rest of the game is easygoing and accessible. It's an enjoyable take on a new classic, even if it won't please everyone.

Want to hear more about the best board games coming out this year? Check out our dedicated guide, or keep up with my reviews in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy of this game was provided by the publisher.

Prior to the debut of Mystery Booster: Commander Edition, I like so many considered myself reasonably well-versed in Magic’s lore. I began my journey with the game back in Aether Revolt, during the rising action of the Bolas Saga, watched videos on older stories in the setting, even played a ripped copy of Shandalar—none of this prepared me for my favorite Commander of the set to be two obscure henchmen from the Onslaught block novels. Sash and Waistcoat, Unmen inspired the same reaction in me as was so eloquently described by one Brian David Gilbert in his treatise on E3 presentations: “What? Hell yeah! What?”. I’m far from alone in saying so, but seeing this set spoiled image by horribly pixelated image was some of the most fun I’ve had when it comes to immediate card reactions. Once the dust settled though, there was one Commander standing above it all, and indeed that was Sash and Waistcoat. Between a modest cost, interesting ability for the table to share, and a shockingly available combo, there’s power hidden in these roaches, waiting to be turned face-up! So much so that we’re actually planning for Bracket 4, something I don’t do lightly here on Commander Focus. What about these Unmen makes me unafraid to start them at high power? Let’s try to understand, together.

"Manifest the top card of your library. Any player may activate this ability."

The first card everyone thinks about when it comes to this pair is Training Grounds, and rightly so—reducing the cost to Manifest all the way down to 1 isn’t just good for you, but makes their first ability all the more appealing for your opponents. That’s not exactly a Bracket 4 mindset, and naturally we have more sinister purposes for a reduced cost ability, but at all levels of power it should be obvious that Training Grounds is the first card to build around for Sash and Waistcoat. The second card, however, is where I differ from most, because there’s but one single other card which reduces an activated ability’s cost by {2}: Power Artifact. S&W isn’t inherently an Artifact, this is true, but there are more than a few ways to get them there, if we even need to. This brings us to the true reason S&W are exciting: If you squint, they’re probably the best mana outlet for Monoblue since Urza, Lord High Artificer. If you make infinite mana, it doesn’t matter what the cost of your Commander’s ability is, and Power Artifact readily combines with Basalt Monolith & Grim Monolith to do just that. On that line of thinking, Rings of Brighthearth doesn’t just give us the ability to basically pay {5} for 2 Manifests by way of S&W, but also make infinite mana with Basalt. Its worst-case scenario is ultimately saving one mana per two activations, which is fine enough. Where things get a bit funny is crossroads at which Sash and Waistcoat's hunt for {2} mana reductions meet the same pioneering spirit on Grim & Basalt. In much the same vein as us turning S&W into an Artifact for Power Artifact, animating a Basalt with Training Grounds around—get this—also makes infinite mana, with it being a Creature and thereby having a reduced cost to untap. All our core combo pieces want the same thing, they just need to swap types around a bit to get there. For Sash and Waistcoat, you're intending to couple that with Ashnod’s Altar to cycle through Manifests (and our entire Library) with a S&W ability that costs {2} or less, meaning that the scariest Artifact to ever hit the board propels another combo machine with a fairly innocuous, cheap outlet in the CZ. You’ve basically got a cheaper, weirder, less stax-reliant build of cEDH’s Power Urza that can go wide in a simplified gamestate. I don’t think S&W are necessarily cEDH material themselves, but borrow those play patterns to do something way, way cooler.

This bridges on the incomprehensible, but trust me this is basically our gameplan.

There’s another wrinkle to this Commander, and that’s in terms psychological. No, I’m not referring to the Kafkaesque art and the effect it may have on those squeamish about pests, but rather the fact that everyone shares in the spoils of your ability’s reduced cost…and position as a mana outlet. S&W get very interesting in B4 because the fact that you can be an opponent’s combo piece means games won’t just end faster, and more explosively, but also involve you far more often as a player. The higher in power level you creep, the more dangerous it is to run S&W out when an opponent could combo off, because as it turns out letting someone Manifest their entire Library is perhaps a bad idea. Moreover, it gives players something to do if stalled, reducing hopelessness and funneling mana into beating down the biggest bad—not you, of course—with unblockable 2/2s. There’s really nothing Faustian about activating S&W as an opponent, especially if you have the mana for it, and you’re far more likely to let things like a Training Grounds live if it appears they could benefit. They shouldn't, of course, but The Selfish Gene is alive and well at the pods in which this Commander sees play. There's an added element of 'Vulture Theory' as well, where in Sash and Waistcoat allowing an opponent to pop off early, and ideally get stuffed, we can try to be the second player to pop off once everyone's burned their interaction. S&W is one of those rare Commanders that gets a ton more interesting at higher Brackets, even if it’s still cool to do things like Manifest Eldrazi and blink them at Bracket ~2.

Statler and Waldorf, Unmuppets

At a baseline, Sash and Waistcoat are indeed just a worse Urza of greater nuance, but the devil’s in the details. I would contend that, in comparing their abilities which serve as mana outlets, their option is far more impactful in the midgame than Urza’s—which often sees use only in the endgame—and that it pulls upon some powerful synergies that have lacked a strong enough home. Foremost among them is a pair of Duskmourn Commander cards, Glitch Interpreter & They Came From the Pipes. Glitch Interpreter was tailor-made for S&W, or perhaps the other way around, turning your unblockable Manifests into a potential 3 cards each turn, on top of having some Acerak-esque combo potential with Ashnod’s Altar. Pipes, meanwhile, just tacks on a draw to each S&W activation, on top of being a phenomenal option to blink, netting two bodies, and therefore two draws, each time it enters. There are other worthy face-down synergy pieces to consider, even at Bracket 4, but the biggest issue is grappling with how bad they are to have in hand, versus hit off of S&W’s ability. Fathom Seer, Kadena’s Silencer, Willbender, Mischevious Quanar, etc are all fantastic to flip at the right opportunity, especially during your combo turn, but they lose a ton of luster if you ever need to pay {3} to play them face down. The agony here is that our buckets of ability cost reduction don't help, as flipping up face-down permanents is a "Special Action", and trades the need of using the stack for not being activated abilities. The issue with Morphs has always laid with that upfront price of {3} for a 2/2, something you’re far happier to pay via Sash and Waistcoat’s ability, rather than a card in hand.

The bug eyes are a design choice.

For that reason, this is far more a deck that cares about putting together its combo than it is a morph/face downs-matter list. We’re playing the best ones, but far more important is flexing S&W’s ability to rip through our Library and blink the best pieces, turning mysterious 2/2s into powerful value engines or pieces of our endgame. We can flex cards like Willbender in much the same way as a deck which draws its Library does, with included free countermagic. It's insulation when you're popping off, with the occasional happy accident of having hidden tricks onboard in the midgame. These also help solve our problem of being a meek little combo deck, with blockers for threats like Tymna and big beaters, encouraging opponents to fight amongst themselves. If we leaned too heavily into incentivizing foes to activate our Commander, such as by playing mass control changing effects or boardwipe buffs, paradoxically it would likely make foes suspicious and less likely to do so. The furthest I’ve gone is in considering Ward of Bones, to lock portions of the game away like playing Creatures & Lands, making S&W’s ability the only way to develop their board, yet unable to attack us. In practice, this led to opponents agreeing not to attack, until we were on the table as a target.

Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, Unalive

There’s a host of ways to make infinite mana in this list, between a Sash and Waistcoat whose ability costs {1} or less and Ashnod’s Altar, Rings+Basalt, or Power Artifact on either Monolith. Navigating those lines isn’t especially difficult, and we can even use a Land released in Murders at Karlov Manner to filter into colored mana throughout the combo, flipping a Branch of Vitu-Ghazi to add {U}{U}, which then allows us to turn a Laboratory Maniac effect face-up and follow that with all manner of draw effects. The slow way is to flex a card like a blinked/bounced and recast Primordial Mists & Nexus of Fate, and kill with unblockable damage (a far sicker path to victory, which requires you play a thematic-but-expensive Enchantment). Absent these paths of play, however, there lies the murky inbetween of Ashnod’s Altar and a S&W ability which costs {2}, discounted by something like Heartstone or Forensic Gadgeteer. Oftentimes we will look to clone these, to acquire our preferred discount of {2}, but you can still steer through the combo with Ashnod's and a 2-cost S&W. This does cycle through your entire Library, sure, but to what end? You can only flip Creatures, inherently, so how are you accessing some other path to victory?

See also: Arthur clenching his fist.

So long as S&W is an Artifact, either works. Let's assume a starting board of S&W, Heartstone (for ease of explanation), Ashnod’s, and three bodies. Keep sacrificing one body to manifest, until you hit Branch of Vitu Ghazi, which we'll flip up by sacrificing another body, floating 1 Colorless mana and turning {3} into {U}{U}. Sac the third body to Ashnods (and recall Branch is now a face-up Land that taps for {C}), retaining the {U}{U}, until you hit a face down Gerrard’s Hourglass Pendant, then spend your Branch's tap and the floating {C} to continue cycling towards a face down Exit Specialist. Spend {1}{U} to flip the Specialist, bouncing the face-down Pendant, then sac your board, cast the Pendant, and bring everything sacrificed previously that turn back to the board tapped. That should provide enough fodder to dig until you hit whatever else you need, so long as you're deep enough; this combo is dependent on the order of your Library, yes, but by virtue of (not kidding) Jack O’Lantern we have an alternate means of finding the {U} necessary for Specialist, even if we’ve played Branch earlier. We need the extra Ashnod fuel to pay for the {1}{U} cost on Specialist’s Disguise. Lines like these are as barebones as possible, as an illustration of your worst-case-scenario of a minimal discount on the Commander. Given any other synergy piece sees “Manifest most of your Library, then bring it back tapped” as a patently absurd path of play alongside any trigger which provides value, it still gets you there. As mentioned though, it is far easier to just go infinite, by way of a {1}-cost S&W ability and Ashnods and/or a Monolith that can untap for {2} or less, and win via Nexus—I’m just showing how savvy pilots can steer the bugs to victory under rationed mana.

Example Decklist: Sash and Waistcoat with Garterbelt

There’s a lot of very cool things going on here, but let’s start by mentioning Relic’s Roar & Behind the Mask. Each of these takes one of the two disparate types for our discounts, being Creatures for Training Grounds/Heartstone, and Artifacts for Power Artifact/Forensic Gadgeteer, and makes the relevant permanent both for the turn. While this can make a card like Power Artifact potentially fall off after that turn, to some extent this works to our benefit, meaning our opponents won’t have the capacity to use a cheap-to-activate S&W on their turns. These are also 1 mana apiece, which is a cost we’re very happy to search, with Dizzy Spell being one of the best means of finding Training Grounds in Monoblue. The very same Micromancer or Spellseeker which finds that Transmute card also has the capacity to grab our ‘wild cards’, and we’re very happy to abuse that. Along the same lines as our Hourglass Pendant, discussed in the above section, is Reenact the Crime; as we cycle through Manifests, this can allow us the opportunity to cast cards Blue normally cannot access from the yard, by virtue of them being Manifested, sacrificed, and then copied.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

This is built as a Bracket 4 list, complete with as many 2-card combos as our funky Commander can muster. To continue that thought, I’ll affirm what I said earlier on in this article: Sash and Waistcoat get more interesting, as relative power level climbs, because forcing the table to play around everyone having a mana outlet is a wildly cool situation to present. S&W are like a Blue take on Heartwood Storyteller, a bane of modern cEDH that's led to ample discussion on the stack as players bicker over a forgotten group hug card, now back with a vengeance. You’re putting a gun on the table, on the bet that you’ll be able to pick it up the quickest, yet it’s arguably cooler to see an opponent try their luck and get stuffed when they attempt to combo off early. As mentioned, ‘Vulture theory’ is in full effect here—it can be to your benefit to be the second person to attempt to combo off, and S&W gives foolhardy foes the chance to be first in line to be interacted-with. If you do drop the Bracket down, suddenly the gun you’re placing on the table isn’t a mana outlet, but instead the ability to go wide with unblockable 2/2s, and that damage can likewise stack up; play cards like Curse of Verbosity, give opponents mana with Victory Chimes, and root for some fun face down gameplay. Heck, you can even try to make it a Timmy list, and flicker some Eldrazi you Manifested.

Un-Axe-cessible

Doug Shuler's original art for Power Artifact is iconic, which is good, given it's stuck on the Reserved List.

More than just being a good Commander, Sash and Waistcoat, Unmen is a fun Commander. There’s elements of some of the best cEDH options borrowed in its play patterns, between Urza, Kinnan, & Thrasios, but I would contend that S&W’s endgames are more interesting problems to solve, and their midgame keeps players engaged who may have otherwise stalled out. While it's not a 1:1 comparison, the feeling of Heartwood Storyteller is present, but instead of being a communal value engine for the table, it's an outlet for decks that might be a card down while assembling an infinite mana combo. What’s crazy about Mystery Booster: Commander is that S&W aren’t even the only 2-mana option with the description of 'communal engine that gets better at high power', as Yume, Chronicler of Valor is also suspect for playability in the 99 of cEDH lists (collusion notwithstanding). On the topic of the set from which Sash and Waistcoat originate, we do need to address the elephant in the room: The way these are being distributed, at time of writing, is disappointing. I don’t think S&W will be one of the truly sought-after Commanders from the set (unless this article blows up, I suppose), but for smash hits like Whtz, the Bibliophile or Homer, the Hermit players who don’t proxy are looking at three-figure price tags for mechanically-unique cardboard. If you’ve gotten this far, you likely do proxy, with Power Artifact being a key card in this list sitting at around ~$120 for a heavily-played copy, and I would contend no set to date makes a better case for getting acquainted with proxies than MB:C. Real-world quibbles aside, I do genuinely urge you to give S&W a try, especially if you enjoy Blue as a color, and high-power Magic as a social experience. You won’t be sandbagging or throwing by playing this list, or this Commander, but that yearning for everyone to ‘do the thing’ is met by providing this communal mana outlet, something no other Commander can do while still being a reasonable pick for true Bracket 4. A measure of altruism can indeed be adaptive, even in the harshest environments.

Until next time, you've activated my trap card, Urza-boy.

title: MTG reveals a Reality Fracture commander that makes Black Lotus tokens
content:
One of the key themes for upcoming MTG set Reality Fracture is the Echoverse, a parallel reality populated by color-shifted versions of famous Magic characters and locations. On Wednesday, Wizards of the Coast revealed the cards for five Elder Sphinxes, powerful magic users who rule over Hexhaven College, the Echoverse mirror to Strixhaven. They're big, flashy legendary creatures who are going to be very popular as Commanders - and perhaps the flashiest of all is Kwia Vigorbloom, a white green Sphinx whose party trick is to create Black Lotus tokens!

Well, to be more accurate, the tokens she creates are simply called 'Lotus' tokens, but they function just the same: each one is a colorless artifact you can tap and sacrifice to create three mana of any one color. Kwia creates one each time you gain life, but there is a big limit on this ability: it can only trigger once per turn. This means there isn't an easy way to set up an infinite loop, though if you find a way to repeatedly flicker her you'll be off to a good start.

Still, this all feels like complaining that my lobster is too buttery. Kwia is a 6/6 flyer with vigilance, lifelink, and ward 2, and if you've got a Soul Warden in play when you cast her she'll immediately refund you half of her six mana cost by making a Lotus. Add in a Panharmonicon effect and you'll ramp away with the game.

If you want a more lasting kind of ramp, Aerid Konstrari is your Sphinx. This red green commander only costs four mana, and in a certain sense doesn't suffer from commander tax. That's because when they enter and when they die you create a Heartwood token, a mana rock that taps for red or green.

Aerid has a six mana ability which creates another Heartwood, and gives Aerid +x/+0 until end of turn, where X is the number of artifacts you control. Starting as a 5/4 flyer, you only have to give Aerid a Sword of X and Y or a Whispersilk Cloak and you're looking at a pretty fast kill by Commander damage.

Denzilore Fatehold is the white blue Sphinx, and the simplest of the bunch. This is a four mana 3/4 flyer with Flash, and a triggered ability - whenever you scry or surveil you put a +1/+1 counter on each creature you know. Go wide with fliers, take all the creatures that let you draw cards when you put +1/+1 counters on them, and find cheap ways to scry. Profit.

The cheapest and weakest of the Sphinxes is Ingris Stingerquill, a mere 1/4 flyer in red and black for just three mana. Don't be fooled - Ingris has a triggered ability that means whenever a creature you control attacks, that creature deals 1 damage to each opponent. Ingris can also create 2/2 colorless Wizard Soldiers and give your whole board haste for four mana, so she can support her own game plan without attacking herself.

My thoughts immediately turn to damage multipliers like Mechanised Assault and Embermaw Hellion, though their damage buffs only apply to red creatures and therefore not the Wizards Ingris is making. If you're up to a deckbuilding challenge, taking Obosh the Preypiercer in the Companion zone is also pretty compelling…

The final Sphinx, the blue black Uldaros Theorix, is great for experienced and inexperienced players alike. When you cast him and he enters, you can exile up to one nonland card of each type from your graveyard, and cast up to six total mana's worth of them for free. Whether you've got a carefully crafted graveyard combo, or you just want to pitch six mana demons into your bin and resurrect them, Uldaros will support you.

Which of these five do you most want to build around, or do you think they'll be better in the 99? How do you think they stack up against the Strixhaven Elder Dragons? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Nintendo's Latest Direct Has Samus Asking: I'm Not Hungry? I Don't Take a Slice?
content:
As we draw closer to the end of the year, that means it is time to start winding down on 2026 gaming news for upcoming titles and start looking forward to the nebulous "2027" release dates, which means it is time once again for a Nintendo Direct recap! This time, Nintendo primarily spent the day trying to sell the Switch 2 as a thing you absolutely need to have or upgrade to, and... maybe did an okay-ish job of doing so, depending on what you're looking for. The console gaming market is looking pretty dire overall, with Sony and Xbox racing to the bottom of a "Duck Season - Rabbit Season - Fire!" routine, but Nintendo has also spent the year spinning their wheels and occasionally sticking their own hands into them. If you missed the Directs (yes, two of them), then we've got the recap to help you on what news you can use for your gaming purchases; we won't be covering everything, so if you want to see the entire directs, we will link both of them here, and focus instead on the things that primarily caught our attention or felt like the biggest news of the day.

Edit 9/10: This article has been updated to include coverage of Level-5's AI made direct, as relevant to discussion of the Professor Layton game below.

Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct

The first direct actually aired the day before, and was devoted entirely to Legend of Zelda. You probably saw the memes and reactions already, but if you didn't, Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake was shown off and looks, uhm... unique? The game has taken a direction that hews especially close to the artistic vision of the directors and stays in line with Zelda's often artistically leaning aesthetic directions, but frankly the game just looks glistening and weird. Link, Zelda, and Ganondorf all look terrible, and I have to admit that I was already kind of on the fence of picking up the remake myself, with this pushing me pretty firmly into "no". Your opinion may vary, so take a look at the trailer yourself and develop your own opinion.

Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity

Age of Calamity didn't really do very well on Switch, but perhaps this time, on Switch 2, things will be different...! Well, it does look better, and if you own the original, an update will be available instead of having to buy the entire game over again. I'm likely going to pass, as even though I enjoy Dynasty Warriors/Musou Games, I didn't really vibe with the Hyrule Warriors games. If you're interested, Age of Calamity Definitive Edition will release on Feb. 25th of 2027.

Nintendo Direct 9/9/26

The other Direct was yesterday's Direct on 9/9, which showed off some of the above Zelda material, as well as a pretty large host of games, with some cool surprises. Overall, I would say the Direct had a somewhat mixed bag in terms of selling the Switch 2; there were some cool games that we'll get to, but nothing that has really been knocking it out of the park in terms of continuing the idea that the Switch 2 is a necessary upgrade from the Switch, except through the fact that less and less games are getting released across both platforms. Since the Switch 2 also has (or attempts to have) parity with other consoles and PCs, there are a lot more multi platform games here that are providing a similar problem that Sony and Xbox are facing, namely, "why do I need this if I have a PC?"

Meccha Chameleon

Developer: Lemorion

Platforms: PC, Switch 2

Release Date: Now!

Meccha Chameleon was all the rage on Twitch a few months ago, racking up a huge amount of sales on Steam as the big flavor of the month game for large friend groups. Essentially hide and seek, Meccha Chameleon tasks players with hiding in various locations and using a fairly robust painting mechanism to try and blend in with the environment. Players accrue points for how long they can hide in view of the hunters, and hunters win by tracking down all of the hiding players. It is very similar to Prop Hunt, and the Switch 2 release was quite a surprise; if you have a large enough friend group of Switch 2 players, this game can be a really fun party game, but you may have better luck on PC.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave

Developer: Intelligent Systems

Platforms: Switch 2

Release Date: September 17

Fire Emblem returns with another huge "main system" installment, following up on 2019's Three Houses and 2023's Engage. Fortune's Weave has players taking on one of four protagonists: Cai, Theodora, Dietrich, or Leda, but don't worry: you still get to create your own avatar (Default named Eshmel) that you can select the gender of before the game begins. Fire Emblem has always been a strong tactical RPG game, and Fortune's Weave is kind of interesting in that it seems to be reviving dungeons, a feature that hasn't been in the main series since Shadows of Valentina. Fire Emblem really tends to attract people for two reasons: the fun rock-paper-scissors strategy combat, and shipping characters together to see what happens. In both cases, I'm ready to play when it comes out next week.

Professor Layton and the New World of Steam

Developer: Level-5

Platforms: Switch, Switch 2

Release Date: Dec. 10, 2026

This one breaks my heart for a simple reason: Developer Level-5 has gone HEAVILY into supporting, promoting, and using AI in their games. Unlike a lot of other nebulous examples, Level-5 also (unhelpfully?) continues to publish their examples for doing so, such as in character art, background art, concept art, programming, and more. So, realistically, I have a hard time supporting their games, which makes the announcement of a new Professor Layton game even more painful for me. Layton is one of my all time favorite series, one that I've bought and played every game in the series for, watched and read just about anything else I can get my hands on from it, and even own a Professor Layton Revoltech that game out years ago. Sadly, while some of this looks great and a return to form, I will need to know what and how AI was used before I can purchase it. The game releases on December 10th, so hopefully we'll find out (and maybe the answer will be it won't have been used, but... not really crossing my fingers). Oh, they also said that Yo-Kai Watch 2: Haunted Domain is in development, if you even care.

Edit 9/10: Man.

So, ignore all of the above. Today, Level-5 held a completely AI made "direct" of their own to talk about the future of the company and show off their CEO's delusional obsession with AI, which was illustrated primarily through the soulless AI created and animated avatar of him that spoke throughout the entire presentation. If you think I'm being hyperbolic, here are some stills of what it looked like:

YOU'RE TOO CLOSE, AI CEO.

What is even happening with almost any of this.

Shaved AI Mario is here. At least his eyes have light to them.

Anyway, as you can see, there's really no hope for any Level-5 games to be unaffected by CEO Akihiro Hino's obsession with AI, and for that reason, you can expect to never see games by Level-5 covered here. It is incredibly disappointing to have to trash Professor Layton, Yo-Kai Watch, and at least personally, Inazuma Eleven, but if you can't even guarantee that your flagship series gets some treatment that doesn't have weird AI mish-mash spellings like BIG FEERY in it, what are we even doing here, man?

You'd think as the maker of Inazuma Eleven, one of THE biggest franchises in Japan, you'd try to ensure all the text actually made sense and not INAZIMA BIG FEERY.

This future sucks man.

Onyx: The Dark Grip

Developer: Bloober Team

Platforms: Switch 2

Release Date: 2027

After Silent Hill 2 Remake, I'm willing to give Bloober a bit more of a benefit of the doubt with games, and their new game Onyx certainly seems interesting. However, the game is being touted as "unplayable" on a television, as it requires use of the touchscreen and possibly motion controls that sucked me out of what otherwise looks like a cool horror puzzle game. I do like the aesthetics and I really do want to give the game a shot, so I hope that the touch and motion mechanics are maybe optional or not that intrusive; while I know these are key tenets of Nintendo systems lately, I've always hated them and find them kind of uncomfortable. We have a while to find out, since Onyx is slated for release some time in 2027.

Ondeh Ondeh: Kaya's Tasty Tale

Developer: Metronomik

Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC, Switch 2

Release Date: 2027

A rhythm platformer, Ondeh Ondeh caught my eye for that reason and the fun aesthetics, and I'm pretty excited to give it a shot when it releases in 2027. Ondeh ondeh is a dish from Southeast Asia, and the game has a lot of that influence present in the presentation overall. It was one of the more original standouts in the presentation, with lots of vibrant colors and an exciting looking world to explore to the music. Also, this one is multiplatform, so almost anyone can pick it up when it releases in 2027.

Metroid Ravenous

Developer: Nintendo

Platforms: Switch 2

Release Date: January 28, 2027

I initially wanted to call today's article "Metroid Prime Vore" but was told no. Anyway, Samus returns in a new 2D game that has her hungry for action as she devours her enemies along the way. If the latest 3D Metroid didn't excite you or interest you, this one seems to be far more along the traditional lines of classic Metroid games, particularly Fusion. The new mechanic presented in Ravenous has to do with the titular adjective: Samus absorbs her enemies powers, adding them to her own arsenal, and in her own words, "It's eat, or be eaten." Judging by the reaction on my personal timeline, everyone has been extremely normal about this.

Dangan Ronpa 2x2

Developer: Spike Chunsoft

Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 and 2, PC

Release Date: January 14, 2027

Dangan Ronpa 2x2 is back, bringing the original Dangan Ronpa 2 kicking and screaming into modernity by also teasing new story paths and gameplay experiences that weren't included in the original, including a brand new character who seems to be a potential new protagonist. If you're not familiar with Dangan Ronpa, the game is essentially a murder mystery and trial game with absolutely bonkers scenarios and a fixation on "Despair" and "Hope" as two driving themes in all of the games. If you've never played them, they can be a lot of fun to give a try, although I'd probably just recommend The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy.

Romancing Saga 3

Developer: SquareEnix

Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 and 2, Steam

Release Date: February 16, 2027

This is probably the biggest surprise for me, and I'm honestly so excited to get to play Romancing Saga again. If you're unfamiliar with the Romancing Saga series, they're sort of like a pervert's final fantasy, in that they have really strange systems, sprawling stories, very unique characters, and a flavor all their own that have mostly been totally impenetrable to Western markets since release; Romancing SaGa 3 came out in 1995, for example, only getting a Worldwide release in 2010. SaGa was a spin-off of Final Fantasy II, which explains why it has so many seemingly esoteric choices in how the games play and how things work; in fact, the very first games in the series were released on Gameboy as "The Final Fantasy Legend" series, which did actually get released in the West. You may also have played SaGa Frontier and SaGa Frontier 2 on PSOne, all of which were strange, weird games. I love SaGa, and I really recommend giving Romancing SaGa 3 a chance when it releases next year; unlike many series, the remasters have all been very good.

Atelier Karia: The Night Kingdom & the Guide of Memories

Developer: Gust

Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, Steam

Release Date: February 25, 2027

Another series for RPG perverts, the Atelier series is a long-storied one in which players are tasked with combining turn-based combat with business management and collection sims to work through an overarching story. Atelier Karia has received a lot of attention recently from a survey in which developer Gust asked players if they would like Karia to get chubby if she ate too much, which resulted in an overwhelming response of "Yes" (80%), proving that good things are actually possible in gaming. Unlike the SaGa series, Atelier has had a pretty wide release in the West, with the latest titles helping the game breach larger audiences thanks to releases on Steam. If you like the idea of a sim-rpg with combat and colorful characters, the Atelier series will fix you right up; if you want to dip your toes into it, consider trying the Ryza series that preceded Karia.

The Apothecary Diaries: The False Imperial Brother

Developer: Gust

Platforms: PS5, Switch 1 and 2, Steam

Release Date: 2027 (Q1)

Speaking of Gust, they also showed off a trailer for their game adaptation of hit period drama and mystery series The Apothecary Diaries, which published originally as a series of Light Novels in Japan before spawning a manga, anime, and live action set of adaptations. Gust makes a lot of sense for a developer to work with Apothecary Diaries; as I mentioned above, they have a big history with simulation and exploration games that are mixed with great stories, and Apothecary Diaries is all about protagonist Maomao's ability to gather and create medicinal solutions or discern the root cause of all sorts of palace intrigue through her mastery of poison and other materials, all while being vexed by the beautiful eunuch Jinshi, who she definitely does NOT have feelings for.

Kirby and the World Beyond

Developer: HAL Laboratory

Platforms: Switch 2

Release Date: Spring 2027

Closing out with the other Nintendo character known for eating people, Kirby is back with a brand new adventure in Kirby and the World Beyond! The newest mainline adventure game brings about Kirby's 30th anniversary of sucking up enemies and stealing their powers, all while exploring cute worlds that also somehow contain horrific secrets and implications. Kirby's newest game seems to follow that tradition, as the lovable and seemingly unbothered cute pink ball is pulled once again into a possibly universe shattering adventure with new characters and a big 3D world to explore, and the trailer shows Kirby running into a new character who he helps by literally cleaving the fake sky entrapping him and others to reveal the world beyond it. I'm absolutely here for it and will be seated in 2027.

Wrap Up...?

There were a lot of other notes and updates in the Direct, namely that Witcher 3 is coming with the updates promised to other platforms, Kingdom Come Deliverance II is getting a Switch release, Monster Hunter Wilds is also on the way with DLC included, and much more. If you'd like to read the nitty-gritty on all of the things announced, you can head over to Nintendo's site and check out the full list of smaller titles and updates, but, in Nintendo Fashion, I have one more trailer I wanted to shout out...

Torneko's Mystery Dungeon Classic HD is out NOW.

Developer: Square Enix

Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 and 2, Steam

Release Date: NOW.

Are you someone who likes the term "Roguelike?" Perhaps you've played various "Mystery Dungeon" games from the likes of Pokémon or series progenitor Shiren the Wanderer? Well, Dragon Quest IV's Torneko is here to explore his own adventure into these styles of games with a game that absolutely vexed a younger Marcy. I absolutely LOVED this frustrating and difficult game's sequel, Torneko: The Last Hope when I played it on the PSOne back in 2000, and although I've played the original since, I had to say this was my favorite announcement of the day, primarily because Romancing SaGa 3 won't be out till next year, and this is out right now. Having already downloaded and played it a bit since the release, I'll tell you that you need to remember how a game from 1993 is going to play, which is to say, slowly and kind of clunky, and I absolutely love it for that. If you want to try a game off my recommendation today, grab yourself a copy of Torneko's Mystery Dungeon. You might regret it at first, but I bet you'll keep playing it till you beat it.

title: D&D mini maker Hero Forge features in a bizarre, hand-painted browser RPG, and it's kind of enchanting
content:
A new Kickstarter featuring Hero Forge miniatures begins funding today, and it promises a pretty weird product. The Dungeons and Dragons miniature maker is officially starring in a videogame. Meet Wildmagic Frontier, a browser-based deck-building, miniature-collecting RPG from Sky Castle Studios. That alone is a pretty novel pitch, but plenty of the game is also hand-painted.

Wildmagic Frontier was first announced in late August. You'll use a collection of Hero Forge miniatures to explore the world of Astara. A former utopia, this land has been reawakened by wild magic. If you have a Hero Forge account, you can import your own creations into the game, though pregen minis allow you to play regardless.

Quests dot the map of Astara, and completing them nets you new mechanics, cards for your deck, and companions for your coterie. When combat inevitably takes place, you'll battle on a detailed diorama - many of these are hand-crafted, with Gaussian splatting technology bringing their textures to the screen.

We don't much more about how the game plays, but creator Sky Castle Studios assures us in a new trailer that Wildmagic Frontier is "a love letter to tabletop". There's dice-rolling, skirmishes, level ups, and plenty of narrative twists and turns - apparently. We can't say how good it actually is until we've tried it ourselves.

For now, all we have is the Kickstarter page. It promises further customization options if certain stretch goals are met. Plus, Wildmagic Frontier will be available through Steam as well as on browser.

title: How to Paint Everything: Marvel Crisis Protocol - Sentinel Prime MK4
content:
Hey everybody, I have returned with a new How to Paint Everything: Marvel Crisis Protocol! This time, I'll be covering how I painted my MK4 Sentinels, which can be found in the new repackaged CP236 Sentinels Affiliation Pack.

For this one, I'll be using the MK4 Sentinel Prime as an example; the standard Sentinel MK4s are still in progress at the time of this writing. But since they are all painted using the same steps, that's perfectly ok. I had painted these big boys once before, in a blue and purple color scheme. But, thanks to Atomic Mass Games sending this pack my way, I get to redo them in a new red and purple scheme that is closer in line to the 90s animated series color scheme.

So, let's get rolling. We have a lot to cover, and this model is basically like painting an action figure from scratch. I'll be going over how I painted the non-metallic metal red and purple effects, as well as a simple drybrushed NMM silver. Finally, I'll cover the glow effects I used for their eyes, chest lights and hand repulsor blasters.

As usual, you'll find a fancy paint chart below. There you'll find all of the colors that were used to paint the Sentinel MK4 miniatures. Let's get to it!

Credit - Brushwizard

Silver Metal Bits

Basecoat - Citadel Chaos Black Spray Primer

Drybrush - AK Interactive French Blue

Drybrush - AK Interactive Snow Blue

Wash - Citadel Nuln Oil

Drybrush - AK Interactive Ivory

Before painting anything else, I started with a primer coat of Chaos Black spray paint. All of the metallic bits were then drybrushed using a large round Army Painter drybrush. I started with a drybrushing of French Blue and another drybrush of Snow Blue. After that, I washed everything with Nuln Oil shade to reinforce the shadows and recesses. Once that was all dry, I gave it all one final drybrushing of Ivory.

Face Plate

Basecoat - Citadel Bugman's Glow

Shadow - Citadel Rhinox Hide

Layer - Citadel Bugman's Glow, AK Interactive Pastel Pink

Highlight - AK Interactive Pastel Pink

The faceplate starts with a basecoat of Bugman's Glow. I then shaded it with a layer of Rhinox Hide, painting this color into all of the recesses. It was also painted on the panels of the face itself, leaving some Bugman's Glow showing. I then mixed Bugman's Glow and Pastel Pink together and painted this mix on top of the other Bugman's Glow areas, to brighten them up. Finally, the panel edges were edge highlighted using Pastel Pink.

Red Armor

Basecoat - Army Painter Basilisk Red

Shadow - Citadel Rhinox Hide

Layer - Army Painter Wyvern Fury

Layer - Army Painter Dragon Red

Layer - Army Painter Dragon Red, Army Painter Angelic Red

Layer - Army Painter Angelic Red

Highlight - Army Painter Angelic Red, AK Interactive Ivory

Highlight - AK Interactive Ivory

Dark Lining - AK Interactive Black

The red armor sections began with a basecoat of Basilisk Red. Shadows were added to the panels by painting Rhinox Hide in the recesses and areas that don't catch direct light. Highlighting started by painting Wyvern Fury on top of the Basilisk Red areas, making sure to leave Basilisk Red showing and blending the two together where they meet. This was repeated using Dragon Red over the Wyvern Fury areas. I followed this up with another layer of Dragon Red mixed with Angelic Red and then a final layer of Angelic Red on its own. Next, I edge highlighted all of the red armor panels with Angelic Red mixed with Ivory, followed by Ivory on its own. The recesses of panel lines were then dark-lined using Black.

Purple Armor

Basecoat - Army Painter Magecast Magenta

Shadows - Army Painter Triumphant Navy

Layer - Army Painter Warlock Magenta

Layer - Army Painter Warlock Magenta, Army Painter Spellbound Fuchsia

Highlight - Army Painter Spellbound Fuchsia

Highlight - Army Painter Spellbound Fuchsia: AK Interactive Ivory

Highlight - AK Interactive Ivory

Dark Lining - AK Interactive Black

The purple armor sections start with a basecoat of Magecast Magenta. Shadows were then added by painting all of the shaded and recessed areas with Triumphant Navy. Next, the I began the highlights by painting a layer of Warlock Magenta, blending it into the Magecast Magenta. Another layer was painted using a mix of Warlock Magenta and Spellbound Fuchsia, followed by a highlight of Spellbound Fuchsia. All of the armor panels were then edge highlighted using a mix of Spellbound Fuchsia and Ivory, and a 2nd edge highlight using Ivory on its own. The recesses were also dark lined with Black.

Chest Light and Eyes

Basecoat - AK Interactive White

Layer - Lethal Shadows Fluorescent Red

Highlight - AK Interactive White

The eyes of the MK4 Sentinels and the light on their chests were first given a base layer of White. They were then given a layer of Fluorescent Red, followed by a highlight of White.

Hand Blaster Lights

Basecoat - AK Interactive White

Layer - Lethal Shadows Fluorescent Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive White

Wash - Citadel Pylar Glacier

The repulsors in their hands were painted White. I then thinned Fluorescent Blue and painted that in the recess, trying to left some white showing in the center. I highlighted the center further using White, and then it was given a wash using Pylar Glacier Contrast paint.

Concrete Basing

Basecoat - Citadel Stormvermin Fur

Stipple - Army Painter Ash Grey

Stipple - Army Painter Brigade Grey

Wash - Citadel Nuln Oil

Like always, my concrete bases start with a basecoat of Stormvermin Fur. Its then stippled with Ash Grey and Brigade Grey. The base is then given a wash with Nuln Oil to tie it all together and shade any recesses in the base.

Rusty Metal Bits

Basecoat - Citadel Mechanicus Standard Grey

Layer - Citadel Doombull Brown

Wash - Citadel Agrax Earthshade

There's a few pieces of wrecked metal on his base. These were given a basecoat of Mechanicus Standard Grey. I then painted thinned down Doombull Brown randomly on them to give the look of rust discoloration. It was finished off with a wash of Agrax Earthshade to tinge the surface brown as well.

credit - Brushwizard

That's the Sentinel Prime MK4 all ready to go! I'm hoping to have the two smaller ones finished up soon, to go along with him. You can find this guy and the other MK4 Sentinels alongside Cassandra Nova in the CP236 Sentinels Affilation Pack, which is now available for purchase at your FLGS or online. As always, a big thank you goes out to Atomic Mass Games and Asmodee for sending this Affliation pack my way. It's very much appreciated!

title: This free Warhammer 40k fan game is a slapstick Space Marine deathmatch
content:
Warhammer 40k's Space Marines have the potential to be every bit as silly as they are epic, a truth the fandom has exploited in everything from comics like Turn Signals on a Land Raider, to made up Space Marine chapters like the Angry Marines, to spoofs like Space King. Grant Howitt, the prolific indie RPG designer behind the incredible Honey Heist, Heart, and Eat the Reich, has had his turn with Falling Angels, a free fangame of slapstick battles featuring barely controlled Space Marines and oh-so-expendable human helpers.

Falling Angels is free to download from the Rowan Rook and Decard website, and fits onto nine short pages. To play, each player needs a Space Marine miniature (or equivalent dude in bulky armor) and a coterie of hangers on. The game is set on a ruined world after the fall of the great space empire, where the last immortal Space Marines now clash with one another in brutal games of martial prowess because, without any real purpose any more, they just want to feel something.

Your marine is supported by a group retinue of mortal lackeys. They're a mixture of lesser warriors and menials with helpful abilities, like a Squire, who can ride shotgun on the back of the Marines' power armor, or a Knight, who can suicidally draw the attention of the enemy Space Marine.

There's some real black comedy here, because these luckless mortals are really here to die. Lackeys are so much weaker than marines that they're prone to burst into showers of gore at the merest touch, while marines can keep fighting despite grievous injuries. But each time one of your retinue makes the ultimate sacrifice, your marine unlocks a new power, making them even more lethal.

The other kind of humor is slapstick. The Space Marines are massive walking tanks, able to Kool-Aid man their way through flimsy breakable terrain. They start the battle slow, with just 4″ movement, but as your retinue starts to die you may be able to increase your marine's Momentum stat. This makes a marine faster, but once they're really motoring they simply can't stop, and they turn like a jeep. Running into a mortal at this speed is like hitting them with a car, while bouncing off an unbreakable obstacle will give the marine a serious headache.

I'm focusing on the humor here, and this is definitely a lightweight narrative game rather than a competitive one, but I can see some interesting tactical grit in it nevertheless. Marines have different arcs just like vehicles in older editions of 40k, and getting into their rear arc or onto the opposite flank from the one that they're holding a shield will be important for survival and actually causing damage. While the rules assume two players going head to head, they seem simple enough that multiplayer battles will be possible.

I haven't tried this yet, but if you do, let me know what you think in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Groundbreaking card game KeyForge announces online version 10 years after its heydey
content:
Ghost Galaxy has announced KeyForge online, a digital adaptation of the decade-old card game. It's expected to launch on Steam in 2028, but the publisher is looking for support via crowdfunding first. A Gamefound campaign will go live "later this year".

KeyForge is a card game released in 2018 by Magic: The Gathering creator Richard Garfield. It pits two players head to head with a pre-made 36-card deck, each of which is totally unique thanks to an algorithm. These decks feature a random combo of three Houses, which decide the playstyle of your deck. You must also declare a House at the start of your turn, as you can only use cards from that category on your turn.

It was a pretty unique prospect, especially back in 2018. Garfield once said he'd been dreaming of developing KeyForge for a decade, but that passion wasn't enough to save the game from a bumpy landing.

KeyForge's original publisher, Fantasy Flight, put the game on hiatus in 2021 after the deck algorithm broke. Ghost Galaxy acquired and revived the game in 2022, and it used crowdfunding to fund three further sets.

The game is alive and well, with its last new release dropping in 2025. But these rough patches did serious damage to the game's visibility. In fact, when I pitched this article, my editor's first response was 'wait, KeyForge still exists?'

KeyForge online might be the most accessible version of the game yet. As developer Yellow King says in a press release: "KeyForge Online brings the unique 'Unique Deck Game' experience of KeyForge to computers, preserving its strategy, unpredictability, and endless deck discovery while adding dynamic visual effects and animations built for video games". "Yellow King aims to build more than just a game: a welcoming online home where new players can discover KeyForge and longtime fans can play, compete, and connect."

The Gamefound page says KeyForge online intends to make existing, tournament-legal decks playable, with additional decks purchasable in-game. More detail will be revealed at KeyForge Celebration 2026.

title: The 10 biggest chase cards in Pokémon TCG 30th celebration
content:
When Pokémon TCG releases its hotly anticipated 30th Celebration set on September 16, it's going to be one of the most epic moments of the year. A Pikachu in every pack! A brand new Futuristic Rare card style! Enough gorgeous illustrator rares to fill a binder! The reveals have been coming thick and fast - now here's our list of the 10 biggest 30th Celebration chase cards every trainer wants to open in their boosters.

30th Celebration is a huge moment for the game, and the Pokémon Company has already revealed a lot of iconic designs that are sure to generate huge demand - we don't expect a single one of these cards to be cheap. But as this is the tentpole release for the whole year, not a niche promo card, it's possible that even the most valuable of these cards will never earn a place in our guide to the rarest Pokémon cards ever. Even so, opening a single one of these cards would be a huge win!

Mew EX and Mewtwo EX Futuristic Rare

1/2

Mew and its cloned relative Mewtwo get what could be their most flamboyant card treatments ever with the new Futuristic Rare cards. When people talk about shiny cards, they don't get much shinier than this! With multi-colored abstract designs on top of multi-hued foiling, they're eye-catching - and the rarest cards in the set. While we'd be overjoyed to open either copy, there's no doubt in our mind that Mew EX is simply better looking. Illustrator YOSHIROTTEN has done incredible work.

Pikachu EX 149 and 150- the day and night party Pikachus

1/2

Cards 149 and 150 in the set are both Pikachu EX, each one partying with a different crew of Alolan Pokémon either by day or at night. If it's the same Pikachu in both cards, this is one party animal! 30th celebration is absolutely bursting with Pikachus, with one guaranteed in every set, and if we were just going off my personal favorite I'd have to go for Pikachu 14/30, illustrated by Okacheke - there's nothing going on in that fluffy head, and I love it.

But in terms of chase cards you'll be glad to open, the Special Illustration Rares are the obvious winners. Both are illustrated by Kantaro, which raises a troubling question - if you're lucky enough to pull one of these beauties, can you possibly chase down the other one to reunite them?

Classic Collection Magikarp Illustrator Rare

Magikarp was among the first ever regular Pokémon to receive an Illustrator Rare card, with this gorgeous card art by Shinji Kanda originally printed in Scarlet & Violet - Paldea Evolved in 2023. The card is being reprinted in 30th celebration with brilliant foiling and a gold shiny border as part of the 'Classic Collection' - a suitably stunning tribute to everyone's favorite useless fish.

Jirachi EX

We have no idea how a Pokémon can be so chilled out while it's embarked on a cosmic voyage, but Jirachi EX certainly is in the art for this SIR. This is a Pokémon living through a galaxy brain meme and somehow still unflappably chill. We don't know how Akira Egawa has made the cosmos seem so vibrant and so trippy, but the effect is stunning.

Zapdos, Articuno, and Moltres IR

1/3

While these are 'only' Illustration Rares rather than SIRs, there's so much going for them. This trio share a gorgeous, extremely clean and bright illustration style by illustrator mashu, which come together to make an inspiring panorama.

Collecting all three parts is going to be about as challenging as getting a specific SIR, but if you've watched Pokémon: the Movie 2000, you'll know how dangerous it is for the world when they're allowed to become imbalanced!

Sylveon EX

Everyone loves Eeveelutions, and this Sylveon EX SIR is an absolute stunner. Although the smiling Sylveon is leaning out of an apartment window, You Iribi has made this feel like a natural scene with the profusion of flower blooms she's summoned.

The way they spiral towards you and seem to reach out to you make this feel like a very welcoming card, with Sylveon holding open a heart-shaped space in the centre. And little touches like the parade balloons in the foreground being a little out of focus make this feel like a photograph a lucky trainer snapped during the celebration!

While these are a mixture of the cards we know will be in huge demand, and team Wargamer's personal favorites, it's far from the full list of secret cards coming in 30th Celebration. Which ones are you most stoked to open in your packs? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: The Paint Review: Ionic x Arnau Lázaro NMM Gold Set
content:
MiG’s Ionic paints have teamed up with world-renowned painter and teacher Arnau Lázaro to create several signature sets, carefully selected to reflect the colours he uses in his work. Ionic kindly sent me the NMM gold set to put it through its paces and see whether it can propel your NMM gold to the next level. I already reviewed the Basic and Expansion sets here.

These 12 paints retail for €42.96, which comes down to €3.58 each, basically the same as if the paints were bought as singles. The set consists of 10 ordinary Ionic paints drawn from the main Ionic range, and two inks:

  • Golden Yellow
  • Primary Yellow
  • Blazing Orange
  • Dark Ochre
  • Dark Skin
  • Slime Yellow
  • Moss Green
  • Vanilla
  • Bubonic Ochre
  • Dark Green
  • Mahogany (Ink)
  • Maple (Ink)

As with the Ionic paints I’ve reviewed in the past, these paints cover smoothly and neatly, with strong colour - though I will say the inks dry a little glossy for my taste, easily solved with varnish, of course, but worth mentioning all the same.

You’ll notice that there are some overlaps between this gold NMM set and the Expansion set (Dark Green & Dark Ochre), but it’s honestly not a big deal since they’re very useful colours to have. As you can probably guess, since the theme is Gold, most of the paints in this set skew towards orange and yellow, with a few greens added to the mix.

Blazing Orange is a fantastic hot orange with an incredible amount of punch that could even reach the dizzying Olympian heights and topple Vallejo Game Color Hot Orange as my favourite orange paint. It doesn’t cover very well, as you might expect; it is an orange, after all. Moss Green is also a really nice paint that I feel would work great as a base for Ork and goblin skin.

An improvement for this set would be the inclusion of some simple step-by-step guides to show the inexperienced how to achieve the effect using the paints in the set. Since the paints are priced very similarly to the single bottles, I feel the value of the set lies squarely in the selection and curation by Mr. Lázaro himself. Following this thread, I feel like the ability of the average painter to make use of this set would have been significantly higher with an included tutorial (either printed in a booklet or as some kind of video) showing the user how to create a gold NMM effect, rather than them having to work out on their own when to use the somewhat–incongruous tones like Dark Green, Moss Green, and Slime Yellow in their NMM practise. As a somewhat seasoned painter, I can guess that the greens are intended to represent the reflection of blue things in gold, like a clear sky or the sea, but whether that would be clear to a novice or intermediate painter, I’m not so sure. If I were to suggest an improvement to the good folks at Ionic, it would definitely be that!

Through this collaboration, Ionic certainly appears to be continuing to pitch itself as a paint brand for the enthusiastic fantasy and sci-fi Display Painter, a category into which (if you read my column A Brush With Greatness, you’ll already know) I fall so neatly that there are hardly any gaps around the edges, so these paints are kind of catnip for me.

Loading...

I began by painting the whole crown with Dark Skin, before layering with successively smaller layers of Dark Ochre, Bubonic Ochre, Golden Yellow, and Vanilla.

I painted some fine edge highlights with Vanilla mixed with a little white, and painted the shadows of the decoration with more Dark Skin, trying to keep them consistent and on the opposite side of the elements to the highlights. Once everything was put together, I glazed the gold areas with some of the Maple Ink to smooth out the transitions and make them sit a little better. It’s rough, for sure, but I think it works as a demonstration and looks pretty nice to boot.

If you’re a figure painter and are looking for a collection of paints for your non-metallic gold work, your choices realistically lie between this set and the Pro Acryl Flameon signature set, both of which are very solid options. I would definitely have liked the inclusion of some kind of instructional content, but as my good friend Mike pointed out, the Flameon set doesn’t offer any instruction either, so that’s just a suggestion rather than a negative point. Compared to the Pro Acryl set, you get double the number of paints for 1 ½ times the price, including the aforementioned greens and oranges to give you more flexibility in your shadows and reflections. Overall, it’s a lot of bang for your buck, and if you’re willing to experiment and figure out just how to use them, this set could be a very powerful tool in your kit.

Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Scythe fans will love this sequel board game, but it has serious problems
content:
Our Verdict

For the right person, Duel of Meloch is a fantastic follow-up to Scythe and Expeditions. It presents the same gameplay, side-by-side in a smooth new system that only asks 45 minutes of your time. It's inventive and impressive, but it's also riddled with design assumptions that make it less enjoyable for inexperienced players to dive into. Combine this with patchy component quality and a mismatch between mechanics and theme, and you've got a mixed bag of success.

Pros
  • Bite-sized version of a great system
  • Tense and fast-paced
  • Inventive concept
  • Endlessly replayable
Cons
  • Abysmal rulebook
  • Easily unbalanced
  • Cheap map
  • Not very thematic

Duel of Meloch is an ambitious crossover between Scythe and its successful sequel, Expeditions. Both are well-loved head-to-head euros from Jamey Stegmaier, but both are very distinct systems. The fact Stegmaier has combined them into such a smooth strategy game is impressive. Despite this, I'm reluctant to rate it highly - because this board game serves a very specific audience.

Duel of Meloch is a two-player game that pits a Scythe faction against an Expeditions one. These are compatible with their games of origin, which means this is technically an expansion for both titles. Things work the other way, too: Stonemaier Games encourages you to mix and match factions from both games to make the mech-battler of your dreams.

To make this work, play is mostly asymmetric. Both players share a double-sided rubber map (which, sadly feels rather unpleasant, and tends to curl at the edges), though each earns different rewards from its hexes. Both share a victory point track, but it's double-sided, and each races to similar yet distinct victory conditions. That race is the core of Duels of Meloch. Each victory point on the track can only be earned once, so securing it blocks your opponent. The first to earn four victory points wins.

Each turn, the two players follow separate gameplay loops. Each is a simplified version of play from the original games. The Scythe player gradually sets up an immense engine by hopping from action to action on their player board. They produce resources, construct mechs, collect cards, and push their popularity and power as high as they can. All these actions can be worth VP with enough investment, but that takes time.

The Expeditions player, meanwhile, can take charge far faster. They move, activate map hexes, and play cards from their hand - or some combination of the three. While there's less of an engine to set up, they grow in potency by collecting new worker abilities for their cards, completing quests, and building upgrades.

Some merging has occurred to keep things smooth. Scythe players can now activate map refreshes like an Expeditions player, while their rival can benefit from Scythe's combat cards.

The combo is functional and, generally, successful. Games last just 45 minutes, and they're as tense as they are smooth. That's mainly thanks to the intricacies of each original system. Both are still tactical, efficient, and excellent, but they don't interact with each other in any meaningful way.

This, too, is built into Duel of Meloch's DNA. I lamented Scythe's lack of player interaction in my original review, and many critics have pointed out how poorly this playstyle communicates the theme of 'big mechs battling for control of alternate 1920s Eastern Europe'.

This disparity feels more apparent here, because this is meant to be a duel. I still think that 'race' is a far better descriptor. Combat is just one way to earn a victory point in Duel of Meloch, and you might be tempted to avoid it completely to pursue a less dicey goal. All other competition happens solitaire. If this is a duel, it's side-by-side rather than head-to-head.

If you're already a fan of the Scythe universe, you've already forgiven this ludonarrative dissonance. You'll find Duel of Meloch to be a fast-paced, fun, and inventive way to re-experience your favorite games. For you, it's the perfect warmup game, in-between session, or palette cleanser. Its replayability will keep you invested for a long, long time.

If you're not already a Scythe convert, you've got far bigger problems than theme.

Duel of Meloch assumes that you're intimately familiar with both Scythe and Expeditions. If that's not true, things start to unravel.

The rulebook is a horrendous experience for the uninitiated. Stonemaier provides a summary of how each side plays, plus some bullet points on what's changed. If that's not clear enough, the publisher also recommends reading the full rulebooks for both original games online, because they're not included in the box.

As a result, the rulebook is hard to follow. It assumes you know what specific symbols and phrases mean, even with the tweaks that make these work in two different contexts. I'd never played Expeditions before testing my review copy of Duel of Meloch, and that meant that the first two or three games were mostly spent flipping through three rulebooks, repeatedly, struggling to find the info I needed.

The assumptions Duel of Meloch makes have a wider impact on balance, too. If an expert Scythe player goes against a novice Expeditions player, they're going to win almost every time. The same seems true in the opposite case. My win rate as the Expeditions player went up significantly once I'd finally sussed out what was going on.

Player experience swings things so dramatically that the game suggests changing its end-game conditions to be easier for the less experienced person. That's a generous addition to the rulebook, but it shouldn't be necessary in a balanced game.

Would I play Duel of Meloch again? Absolutely. When armed with the right know-how, it's the kind of puzzle you delight in unpicking. I expect the expert Scythe players will love it even more than I did. I'd just love it way more if the price of entry wasn't so damn high. I'm fond of games that reward players for becoming expert; I'm less fond of games that require this expertise to function.

Want to learn more about this year's best board games? Check out our regularly updated guide, or hit me up for my top picks in the Wargamer Discord.

A review copy of Duel of Meloch was provided by the publisher.
